German writer tells of Chinese spy in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:46:18 UTC
01:46:18 KST

A German veteran journalist and author said the Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau (MJIB) has confirmed his suspicion that he was followed by a Chinese spy on Alishan (阿里山) last year.
Jurgen Kremb, who has long researched Chinese intelligence agencies, Asian geopolitics and cross-strait relations, made the comment during an interview with Taiwan Plus on Sunday.
A video of the interview was subsequently shared by the Canadian Trade Office in Taipei on its Facebook page.
Photo: Screen grab from Taiwan in Canada’s Facebook page
Kremb said that last year, while writing a report on Chinese espionage activities targeting Taiwan, he traveled to Alishan with friends. A young Asian woman approached them and struck up a conversation, but Kremb immediately noticed that she spoke with a distinctly northern Chinese accent rather than a Taiwanese one.
He said he was even more surprised when they returned to their hotel and found the woman sitting in the lobby, directly beside one of his colleagues.
He said he immediately warned his friends that she was an intelligence agent from China, and told them to stop talking on the phone.
Although his friends were initially skeptical, Kremb said his experience as the former editor-in-chief of a German magazine and his years working in China had taught him how to quickly identify intelligence operatives.
After returning to Taipei, they reported the incident to the investigation bureau. The bureau reviewed surveillance footage and confirmed that the woman, who had not checked into the hotel, had followed them, hiding behind cars and around street corners, Kremb said.
After the bureau intervened, the woman left Taiwan two days later, he added.
Kremb said he had faced daily surveillance and intimidation while working in China and was eventually expelled after developing reliable sources.
His experience has given him a clear understanding of Chinese intelligence operations, and he has even written a book about German intelligence agencies, he said.
He added that he was surprised to see similar surveillance and intimidation tactics being used in Taiwan.
“Seeing this with my own eyes in Taiwan felt like a warning,” he said. “I was not shocked, but I was very surprised.”
The MJIB yesterday confirmed the account of being followed and subsequently reporting the incident, as described by Kremb, was accurate.
It said it launched an investigation after receiving the report last year, but declined to provide further details, citing restrictions on disclosing information about an ongoing investigation.
The incident shows China has long carried out transnational repression worldwide, targeting not only Chinese and Taiwanese, but anyone who opposes communist authoritarianism or advocates democracy, freedom and human rights, it said.
Taiwan will continue working with democratic partners to counter China’s extraterritorial reach and transnational repression, it said.

New Taipei opens cat-friendly space to promote pet care, adoption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:46:17 UTC
01:46:17 KST

New Taipei City yesterday opened what it said is Taiwan’s first cat-friendly "demonstration and education space," where prospective adopters and existing cat owners can interact with shelter cats and learn how to provide a suitable home environment for the animals.
The Happy Meow Home (幸福喵樂宅), which opened in the Banciao (板橋) public animal shelter, includes a mock home designed around cats’ behavioral and physical needs and an educational area covering topics such as preparing for adoption, daily care, and health and aging.
The space was designed to help people understand "not only how to interact with cats, but also the kind of environment cats need," said Pao Hai-ni (鮑海妮), deputy director of the city’s Animal Protection and Health Inspection Office.
Photo courtesy of the New Taipei City Government via CNA
The mock home demonstration area, where three shelter cats are staying, includes elevated platforms, hiding spaces and gentler slopes for older cats, along with examples of litter boxes and water bowls, she said.
The city hopes the facility will help owners understand how to provide cats with a better living environment and "accompany them into old age," Pao said.
It would also give prospective owners the chance to interact with a cat before adoption, helping them figure out whether they are a good match and reduce the risk of animals later being returned or abandoned, she said.
Visitors can reserve a roughly 30-minute session to interact with cats in the mock home, with about six to eight groups accommodated each operating day — Tuesday through Sunday — due to limited space and to avoid overwhelming the cats.
Those who need English-language assistance can indicate so when making a reservation, and a volunteer would be arranged to help, Pao said.
During the sessions, visitors are encouraged to let the animals initiate contact.
"We don’t want people to grab the cats. We let the cats slowly approach them, because that is what really conforms to cats’ natural behavior," Pao said.
Only cats that have adapted to the environment and are comfortable around strangers would be brought into the area, she said.
New Taipei City Mayor Hou You-yi (侯友宜), who attended yesterday’s opening, said that about 370,000 dogs and cats are registered in the city, including nearly 180,000 cats, with the number of new cat registrations in the past few years being more than double the number of dog registrations.
The trend mirrors a broader shift across Taiwan. A Ministry of Agriculture survey last year estimated the country’s pet cat population at 1.74 million, up 32.8 percent from about 1.31 million in 2023, while the estimated pet dog population fell 1.2 percent to about 1.46 million.
There are 142 cats and 823 dogs available for adoption at the city’s eight public shelters, while 2,879 cats and 876 dogs were adopted over the past year, Pao said.

A deadly stampede yesterday broke out at a Hindu temple in eastern India’s Bihar state, hours after a fire swept through a hotel housing pilgrims in West Bengal state.
Seven people were killed and more than a dozen injured in the stampede, while the blaze left at least seven people dead and several others critically injured, police said.
The incident in Bihar occurred near Ashok Dham Temple in Lakhisarai District, as thousands of devotees gathered to offer prayers on the third Monday of Shravan.
Photo: AP
The period, which usually falls between July and August, is dedicated to the worship of Hindu god Lord Shiva and is marked by fasting, prayers and colorful monsoon festivals across the nation.
More than a dozen people were taken to a government hospital for treatment, the Press Trust of India news agency quoted civil official Shailendra Kumar as saying.
The cause of the stampede was still being investigated, he added.
An electric wire snapped outside the temple premises at about 6:30am, sparking panic as devotees rushed to escape what they feared was a risk of electrocution, preliminary reports said.
A section of the barricades collapsed under the weight of the surging crowd, leading to a crush in which people fell over one another, Kumar said.
In Tarapith, a temple town in West Bengal’s Birbhum District, a fire broke out at about 4:30am on the ground floor of a four-story hotel while most guests were asleep, the Press Trust of India reported.
Many of the guests were pilgrims visiting Tarapith to offer prayers where a major temple complex also includes a shrine dedicated to Lord Shiva. Firefighters brought the blaze under control and the injured were taken to a hospital where some were being treated for burn injuries while others suffered from smoke inhalation and asphyxiation, the report said.
Hotel management told the news agency that the blaze might have originated near the reception area after an electrical component in the hotel’s power supply system caught fire. Authorities are investigating the incident and have not yet established the exact cause.
Crowd crushes are relatively common in India during religious festivals, as large crowds, sometimes in the millions, gather in confined areas with few safety or crowd control measures.
In January last year, at least 30 people were killed as tens of thousands of Hindus rushed to bathe in a sacred river during the Maha Kumbh Festival, the world’s largest religious gathering.
In 2013, pilgrims attending a Hindu festival at a temple in the central state of Madhya Pradesh panicked amid fears that a bridge would collapse. At least 115 people were crushed to death or drowned in the river below.

Monitoring rules ‘unreasonable,’ officers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:46:14 UTC
01:46:14 KST

A number of police officials have described the rules requiring commanders to monitor officers on unpaid leave as “unreasonable” following a case in which an officer was fired for allegedly working as a male escort while on unpaid leave.
The man, surnamed Chuang (莊), who worked as a male escort at a host club while on unpaid leave, was fired after being accused of defrauding a female customer of NT$1 million (US$31,395) and leaking police information to another client after returning to duty.
Chuang was indicted over the allegations, given two major demerits and dismissed from the police force.
Photo: Taipei Times
Commanders at all levels are responsible for monitoring serving officers, suspended officers and those on unpaid leave, including keeping a close watch on their work, personal lives, conduct and behavior, according to the Regulations Governing Police Discipline (端正警察風紀實施規定).
When reached for comment, a number of senior police officers have criticized the requirement as impractical, saying that supervisors already struggle to oversee active-duty officers, let alone those on extended leave.
Supervisors could at most make telephone inquiries, and they have no way of verifying the truth if the person gives evasive answers, they said.
Given the heavy workload of police duties, requiring supervisors to conduct home visits would increase administrative burdens without guaranteeing results, they said.
There have been cases in which off-duty officers became involved in alcohol-fueled disputes and fights that made headlines, a precinct chief said.
Supervisors are not babysitters and cannot follow personnel around 24 hours a day, he said.
Supervisors are typically held accountable when officers under their command commit misconduct and face disciplinary action, a police inspector said.
However, the Code of Conduct for Police Personnel (警察人員獎懲標準) also stipulate that supervisors could be exempt from disciplinary responsibility when officers are objectively beyond effective supervision for more than one month due to training, study, leave, suspension or unpaid leave.
While the supervisor in Chuang’s case was exempt from disciplinary action, the scandal has allegedly prompted police departments nationwide to order local unit heads to increase outreach and lifestyle monitoring for personnel on leave.
Many disciplinary rules originated from a longstanding practice of collective responsibility inherited from the military, police officials said.
As officers have become increasingly conscious of their rights, calls are growing to update these regulations and eliminate the provisions.
Officers on unpaid leave remain civil servants and while taking part-time work is not entirely prohibited, they must comply with the Civil Servant Service Act (公務員服務法), and cannot engage in work that could damage the reputation of civil servants or the government, or contravene rules prohibiting them from running businesses, a police inspector said.
If an officer takes unpaid leave to care for a newborn, they could use their free time to work part-time at a convenience store, make deliveries, run an online business or do programming from home, the police inspector said.
However, they cannot take on a full-time job or work such long hours that they are unable to care for their child, nor can they engage in work that could damage the image of civil servants, such as working at a casino, hostess club or arcade, he added.

Invasion is an existential gamble for Xi, expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:46:14 UTC
01:46:14 KST

A full-scale Chinese invasion of “the unsinkable fortress” of Taiwan would be an “existential gamble” and could become Beijing’s biggest mistake, The Sun reported on Saturday, citing former British diplomat Charles Parton.
If Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) fails to take Taiwan, he “risks being swept away by the reaction from the mainland,” said Parton, senior associate fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute.
His biography on the institute’s Web site says he spent 22 years working in or on Taiwan, China and Hong Kong.
Photo: Xinhua news agency via EPA-EFE
In addition to anger among Chinese who would lose their children in the war, the Chinese economy would likely collapse, and the resulting “great economic dislocation” would lead to unemployment, leaving Xi’s reputation for good governance “in tatters,” he said.
Parton called this an “enormous risk” and said he would be “very surprised” if Xi would pursue it “without being close to 100 percent sure he would win in Taiwan.”
If Taiwanese are properly prepared, “it would be extremely difficult to invade and the chances are that you wouldn’t succeed,” he said, adding that Chinese forces would have the “extremely difficult” task of crossing 161km of rough waters to reach Taiwan’s well-defended islands.
Parton said China has only about 13 beaches where forces could feasibly land on and that any airborne troops “are at great risk of being shot out of the sky, particularly as drone technology increases.”
Beijing would have to muster vast numbers of troops, materials and air support for an invasion, a buildup that would be a “pretty clear warning,” he said.
“This would give time for the Americans and others to reinforce and make it even more difficult for China,” he said. “So I am very doubtful that there would actually be an invasion.”
If China attempts to blockade Taiwan, it would essentially cut off much of the Taiwan Strait, a crucial shipping lane for the global economy, he said.
“There would be an economic meltdown globally” and “a massive downturn” in China, Parton said.
“And then you get into a scenario of mass unemployment in China,” he said.
Parton described the situation as an “existential threat,” citing “massive unemployment and massive instability aimed at the party.
Even if China could occupy Taiwan, it would be difficult to hold on to because of prolonged guerrilla resistance, he said.
Parton said that Xi could think: “If we’re going to go through months, years of guerrilla resistance then this is not going to look good with my people.”
China is much more likely to continue putting other forms of pressure on Taiwan to convince Taiwanese that unification is inevitable, he said.

Executive Yuan appoints Wen NCC representative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:46:12 UTC
01:46:12 KST

The Executive Yuan on Thursday last week appointed National Communications Commission (NCC) Secretary-General Wen Chun-yu (溫俊瑜) as the agency’s representative to maintain the commission’s basic operations after the terms of the last three commissioners expired on July 31, leaving all seven posts vacant, the NCC said yesterday.
The move was intended to protect the public interest and people’s rights by ensuring the regulator can continue performing essential functions, the commission said.
The NCC said it would handle matters in accordance with the rules governing issues that can be handled by internal units under delegated authority.
Photo: Tsai Ssu-pei, Taipei Times
Under the arrangement, the NCC would prioritize cases affecting people’s daily lives and issues of major public interest, including import approvals for telecommunications-controlled radio-frequency control equipment.
The commission would compile a weekly list of cases handled during the leadership vacuum and submit them for review once a new group of commissioners takes office.
The lack of an authorized agency representative had prevented the NCC from formally issuing documents, including import approvals for radio-frequency equipment and licenses, the commission said.
As a result, 280 official documents and 269 equipment approval and licensing cases were left pending, it said.
Contractual payments could not be made either, affecting people’s rights, it added.
Wen said the agency would expedite the issuance of licenses and fulfill outstanding contractual obligations.
The NCC said that a sizable cut to its administrative budget could further undermine its ability to operate normally.
The legislature cut NT$57.823 million, or 56 percent, from the NCC’s budget for basic administrative operations from this month through December. The funding covers essential expenses such as electricity and water, telecommunications, rent, building security, cleaning and equipment maintenance.
The NCC said it faced a similar situation last year, when NT$37.589 million, or 50 percent, of its operating budget was cut.
The shortfall was later covered through a supplementary budget.
With its administrative funding again substantially reduced while all commissioner posts remain vacant, the NCC warned that its normal operations could be seriously affected.
Staff would remain at their posts and maintain operations despite the unprecedented challenges, the commission said, adding that it hopes the legislature would complete its review of seven commissioner nominees as soon as possible so the agency can return to normal operations.

The importance of self-criticism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:46:10 UTC
01:46:10 KST

Discussions of “cognitive warfare” in Taiwan often take an overly sensitive stance without ever taking the lead in setting the agenda. Many Taiwanese fall back on simplistic apologetics and complacent assurances that everything is fine. The underlying premise seems to be that as long as Taiwan projects an image of strength, there will be no cracks for China to exploit.
When seen from Beijing’s perspective, the flaw in this logic becomes apparent. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) relies heavily on positive messaging and tightly managed information to maintain political stability. Taiwan simply cannot beat an authoritarian state at its own game.
However, it can adopt a different approach in the battle of narratives: Acknowledge shortcomings to build trust and frame the debate in ways that Beijing cannot control. A friend of mine serves as editor-in-chief of a Taiwanese newspaper that takes a hawkish position on national defense and favors a stronger military. The paper maintains an official account on X, where its editors noticed an interesting phenomenon. Posts arguing that Taiwan was losing the arms race with China frequently spark a vocal backlash from fiercely pro-CCP users.
At first glance, this seems counterintuitive. It might be assumed that criticism of Taiwan would please Beijing, but the opposite happened instead. Criticism matters not only for what it says, but for where it leads. If criticism of Taiwan’s weaknesses provides an incentive for the nation to bolster its armed forces, improve its defense-industrial base and build a more resilient manufacturing infrastructure, then Beijing has reason for dismay.
A narrative that isolates areas in which Taiwan is weak and in which improvements need to be made, does not serve Beijing’s interests. It backs Beijing up against a wall. The communist party line is that Taiwanese society is suffused with defeatism and welcomes “a return to the motherland.”
If Beijing openly attacks Taiwanese voices calling for stronger defense, it risks undermining its own propaganda directed at the domestic audience. Such a condemnation would also affirm another truth for Taiwanese: The best and arguably only way to resist the threat from China is through greater military preparedness, stronger deterrence and a harder line against Chinese pressure. That is not the conclusion Beijing wants Taiwanese to draw.
Taiwanese commentators can openly ridicule Chinese military problems such as alleged crashes of advanced aircraft or photographs of a carrier emitting heavy exhaust during Chinese military exercises around Taiwan in August 2022. Beijing does not have the same luxury to mock comparable Taiwanese mishaps, such as when a vessel in the Coast Guard Administration’s 35-tonne patrol-boat construction program sustained a main-engine failure or when the coast guard displayed excessive caution by not using the Zhenhai multiple-rocket system during law-enforcement operations.
If Beijing were to scoff at the Republic of China military, it would be implicitly acknowledging that Taiwan and China are engaged in a military competition of opposing sides of equal rank rather than accepting Beijing’s preferred political narrative that “the Taiwan problem” is simply an internal matter.
Another blow to the CCP propaganda machine is that serious criticism of Taiwan’s defense establishment inevitably goes beyond individual equipment. It raises questions about bureaucratic rigidity, risk aversion and an institutional mentality that often prioritizes preventing mistakes over encouraging initiative or expanding capability. In other words, Taiwan has a bureaucratic culture that can become so concerned with avoiding problems that it becomes reluctant to get things done.
China suffers from many of the same problems. The difference is that China is an authoritarian state. Its officials do not have to worry about the risks involved in preventing abuse, so the CCP can sometimes push projects forward with fewer restraints. Aside from that, the same fear-based, responsibility-adverse bureaucratic rigidity is also rife in China.
Therefore, if the CCP dares to criticize Taiwan along these lines, the resulting public discussion could just as easily turn into a mockery of the Chinese government’s own institutional failures. None of Taiwan’s major opposition parties takes a tougher line toward China than the ruling party. If self-criticism is framed specifically around the effectiveness of such a stance, then opposition parties would find it politically difficult to attack that degree of introspection — and China even more so.
The purpose of self-criticism is not to denigrate Taiwan. It is to turn those weaknesses into arguments for military reform, institutional improvement and greater national resilience. Taiwan should not simply wait for China to establish the terms of cognitive warfare and then scramble to defend itself. It should define the terrain itself with honesty and purpose.
Wang Wen-sheng is a retired political operations officer and doctoral candidate researching the history of Australia’s and New Zealand’s ties with Oceania.
Translated by Amy King
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.
China’s new exit and entry regulations might signal an increase in the risk that Taiwanese travelers will face, an analyst said on Tuesday last week. The new rules, which take effect on Sept. 15, expand the power of authorities to restrict travel on national, industrial and technological security grounds, question travelers about their reasons for leaving and inspect electronic data. Taiwanese who do not support the ruling party should not dismiss the warnings as fearmongering or propaganda. Man ordered to pay NT$400m after hypermarket arson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:46:10 UTC
01:46:10 KST

The Taoyuan District Court has ordered a 22-year-old man to pay about NT$400 million (US$12.6 million) in damages after he set fire to a hypermarket in Taoyuan two years ago.
The man, surnamed Kuo (郭), went to the hypermarket along with two friends, surnamed Huang (黃) and Chou (周), early on Dec. 3, 2023, said the ruling handed down on July 31.
Kuo used a lighter to set fire to a bottle of insecticide spray in the cleaning supplies section on the first basement floor and put it back on the shelf, the ruling said.
Photo: Taipei Times
The three continued to shop in other sections of the hypermarket when the fire on the spray bottle ignited other pesticides and caused explosions, it said.
The fire soon spread to other areas, and seriously damaged the wall and ceilings of the first and the first basement floors, it said.
The severely damaged hypermarket had to suspend operations for about half a year.
There were eight insurance companies seeking a total of more than NT$398.27 million in damages, and they have jointly filed a subrogation claim against Kuo.
Kuo must pay more than NT$398.27 million in damages, the court ruled.
As the fire also affected a nearby coffee shop, an insurance company filed another subrogation claim against Kuo to recover NT$979,326 in compensation. The court ordered Kuo pay the entire amount.
Kuo was sentenced to six months in jail on conviction for arson that destroyed an occupied building.
He did not attend his oral argument hearing, nor did he submit a written statement.
The judge found the insurance companies’ claims to be substantiated after considering the evidence and investigation results.
The ruling can be appealed.

Cuts hamper fight on Chinese disinfo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:46:10 UTC
01:46:10 KST

Heavy cuts to government media budgets in this year’s general budget would weaken Taiwan’s ability to counter Chinese disinformation and cognitive warfare, a researcher said on Sunday.
The legislature on Friday passed the central government’s annual budget, but slashed the media budgets of all government agencies by 50 percent.
The Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) was hit with an even deeper cut, with its media budget cut to about NT$1.5 million (US$47,093) from NT$12.95 million.
Photo: Taipei Times
It is the council’s job to analyze China’s policies toward Taiwan, “united front” tactics and cross-strait risks and communicate its findings to Taiwanese, said Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), deputy executive director of Tunghai University’s Center for Mainland China and Regional Development Research.
The deep cut to the council’s media budget would hinder its ability to communicate the information it gathers and analyzes and make it easier for Chinese messaging to gain influence in Taiwan, he said.
In its cognitive warfare efforts against Taiwan, China uses social media and exchanges to spread narratives that influence how Taiwanese view cross-strait relations, Hung said.
The government needs the resources to verify information and communicate with Taiwanese, he said.
The cuts weaken the government’s ability to counter China’s “united front” tactics and cognitive warfare through public communication and information campaigns, he added.
The MAC needs to communicate effectively with diverse groups facing different risks, including people traveling to China for tourism, study, work, business or exchanges, Hung said.
The cuts would limit the MAC’s reach and the channels available to it for targeted communication, making it harder for the council to get relevant information to those who need it, he said.
The legislature has the right to scrutinize government spending and review the effectiveness of media budgets, including asking agencies to explain or improve how funds are used, but cutting the council’s media budget to just 12 percent of its original amount is excessive, Hung said.
Taiwan would ultimately bear the cost of wider information gaps and greater risks from the cuts, he said, adding that this is a result China would welcome.
The cuts to the MAC’s media budget would make it harder for the government to inform people about China’s actions toward Taiwan, potential risks of traveling to China and changes to Chinese laws, Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Chang Hung-lu (張宏陸) said.
Without this information, Taiwanese could be at risk while traveling in China and Beijing would have an opportunity to claim it has jurisdiction over Taiwan, Chang said.

Xi leads event marking Jiang Zemin’s birth centenary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:45:51 UTC
01:45:51 KST

Top Chinese officials led by President Xi Jinping (習近平) yesterday gathered in the Great Hall of the People in Beijing to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the birth of late leader Jiang Zemin (江澤民), who led China in a pivotal phase in its rise from a marginal economy to a global economic power.
Jiang, who died in 2022 at the age of 96, led the country through a decade of rapid economic growth after the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown on pro-democracy protesters.
His co-partner in governance, former premier Zhu Rongji (朱鎔基), died last week, with the funeral scheduled today.
Photo: Reuters
The passing of the two leaders marks a definitive end to the reforms that both represented during the 1990s and early 2000s, with more emphasis on private entrepreneurship and wealth creation.
That stands in contrast to Xi, who has exerted greater central control and pressed a state-driven economic policy focused on technological autonomy and strategic industries.
In a 40-minute speech, Xi called on the Chinese Communist Party to carry forward Jiang’s legacy, presenting the current leadership as the continuation of his political and ideological project.
That message was also carried in state media coverage in the past few days.
Under Jiang and Zhu, China pushed through painful changes: shuttering unprofitable state firms, dismantling the old housing system in favor of a commercial property market, weathering the Asian financial crisis of the late 1990s and joining the WTO in 2001.
Xi now faces challenges of his own as he seeks to weather trade frictions with the US and Europe, tensions over Taiwan, slower economic growth and demographic decline.
“On the new journey ahead, we must heighten our sense of vigilance against potential dangers,” Xi said.
“With an indomitable fighting spirit and superb skill in struggle,” we must “proactively meet the major tests posed by high winds and rushing waters, or even by raging storms,” he added.
Events involving Xi are closely monitored by China watchers for clues to the political pecking order, and for indications of the health and continued standing of the country’s retired elite.
Former Chinese president Hu Jintao (胡錦濤), Jiang’s immediate successor, now 83, was not immediately seen in state media footage of the event, which was attended by current and retired officials.
Hu’s premier, Wen Jiabao (溫家寶), as well as former vice president Wang Qishan (王岐山), Xi’s one-time anti-corruption chief, were seen at the event, suggesting that they remain in favor with the leadership.
A number of officials once associated with Wang have come under corruption probes in recent years.

Ebola outbreak breaks record in DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:45:50 UTC
01:45:50 KST

Ebola deaths were recorded at a rate of one every 28 minutes in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) last week, making the outbreak the nation’s deadliest on record as authorities struggle to contain the rapidly spreading disease.
The death toll reached 2,325 after another 365 fatalities were recorded last week, surpassing the 2,299 deaths during the nation’s record Ebola outbreak in 2018-2020.
Almost 5,000 confirmed infections have been reported since the current outbreak was declared in May, the National Institute of Public Health said on Sunday.
Photo: AFP
The epidemic is doubling about every 20 days and the response needs to expand substantially to regain ground, UN Under-Secretary-General for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator Tom Fletcher said on Friday.
Authorities and aid groups need to double the number of teams conducting safe burials, triple treatment capacity, improve contact tracing and deploy more experienced managers, he added.
“Ebola is winning in the Democratic Republic of the Congo,” he said. “We cannot let the virus outrun our response.”
Fletcher announced an additional US$30.5 million from the UN’s Central Emergency Response Fund on Friday, on top of US$24 million already allocated to the nation and neighboring countries.
The UN has deployed another 20 humanitarian staff to the outbreak’s epicenter, while the World Food Programme is expanding food assistance at Ebola treatment centers.
The pressure is spilling into ordinary hospitals and clinics. Dedicated beds for suspected Ebola patients in North Kivu Province were fully occupied by Saturday, while suspected cases in Butembo, Masereka, Vuhovi and Kalunguta were being isolated in existing health facilities that were not designated transit centers, the institute said.
The virus poses particular risks for health workers. Ebola had infected at least 155 of them and killed 45 by Aug. 9, the WHO said in a report on Friday.
The infections highlight persistent weaknesses in infection prevention and control, particularly outside designated Ebola treatment centers, the agency said.
Ebola is hitting a health system already weakened by years of conflict and mass displacement, with recent cuts to humanitarian funding adding to the strain.
Hospitals and health centers in parts of North and South Kivu are operating with fewer staff, medicines and supplies, while some have suspended operations because of violence, Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) said.
Measles, cholera, malaria and other health emergencies risk being neglected as resources are mobilized against Ebola, MSF said last week. DR Congo had recorded 108,643 suspected measles cases and 1,394 deaths through July 19, as well as 35,464 suspected cholera cases and more than 1,050 deaths.
Fear of Ebola is also deterring some people from seeking care, potentially delaying treatment for other illnesses, the group said.
“We are putting the world on notice that the Ebola crisis is real,” Fletcher said. “This is now everybody’s problem.”

Modern war is systematically erasing human history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:45:48 UTC
01:45:48 KST

Wars might not take summer holidays, but they do sometimes see exhaustion. As drones race back and forth across Ukraine and the Strait of Hormuz, a grim stalemate seems to have invaded the earth beneath. Aerial bombardment knows limited resistance and even less victory or defeat. Ukraine, Russia, Israel, Iran and their allies seem able to defy diplomacy and drop bombs on each other for ever.
At which point the outside world can merely count some of the costs. Russian President Vladimir Putin’s known desire to eliminate Ukraine’s historical identity has led to its cultural devastation. Two weeks ago, UNESCO reported the destruction or dereliction of 545 of its historic buildings, including 156 religious sites and 43 museums. The attempted eradication of what Putin himself claims to be an intrinsic part of Russia’s own history is sickening.
Russia’s bombing of Kyiv’s Pechersk Lavra complex and the Dormition Cathedral, coupled with shattering the magnificent St Sophia Cathedral, are comparable to Ukraine bombing the Kremlin. So, too, is the attack on a cathedral and a museum in Odesa, and the destruction of a theater in Mariupol. These are defining monuments of Ukraine’s past. Yet their dereliction has received little publicity in the West.
Meanwhile, in Iran, the beautiful city of Isfahan might surely have been spared US President Donald Trump’s egotistic bomb-fest. Not so. A Reuters survey in June found the historic Naqsh-e Jahan Square, the Jameh Mosque and the governor’s palace partially destroyed. In Tehran, the Persian royal palace of Golestan has been badly damaged. UNESCO reports of an attack on an 1,800-year-old fortress that embraced a prehistoric settlement reputedly 63,000 years old.
The most savage consequence of the collapse of order in the Middle East is the reported damage or destruction of over 80 percent of the buildings in Gaza. The ancient city of Gaza itself is now largely rubble. Bombed by Israel are the medieval Great Omari Mosque and the Church of St Porphyrius, dating from the fifth century and one of Christianity’s most ancient sites.
Gaza’s archives have been destroyed. The Omari Mosque’s library and the adjacent cultural center, whose thousands of ancient documents had survived the Crusades, have reportedly been lost. The al-Qarara Museum was bombed from the air and then bulldozed to the ground. A people’s entire past has been deliberately eradicated.
As for Israel’s war on Lebanon, it culminated in June in what appeared to be the gratuitous bombing of the ancient port of Tyre. This included an attack on the site of the Roman hippodrome. The 1,000-year-old fortress of Beaufort was also damaged. The past is clearly without privilege.
Aerial wars are unlike ground ones. Soldiers with guns have targets. So, we are constantly told, do modern missiles, but that does not explain the US bombing of an Iranian girls’ school in February. The reality is that bombers are casual, because they are near invulnerable, while their victims appear small and anonymous. Bombers do not conquer territory or secure surrender. They are manifestations of leadership machismo.
In the allied invasion of Italy in 1943-1945, British and US officers were known to take steps to protect its monuments from destruction. As a result, Italy’s ancient cities survived to a degree that Germany’s did not. In the aftermath, sincere efforts were made to evolve rules of war, including respect for cultural and historic monuments. War was still seen as a contest of professionals, not of cultures.
The result was The Hague Convention of 1954 and the Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in 1972. However, in the past few years, in which we have seen a collapse of global governance, have left The Hague Convention a paper tiger, like that other supposed discipline, the UN’s International Court of Justice. Victory today appears to lie in destroying an enemy’s identity and morale as much as in killing its people. When the Islamic State ruined much of the Iraqi city of Mosul in 2014, it set about eliminating all traces of its past. Trump’s threat to Iran, that “a whole civilization will die tonight,” showed an equally primitive approach to conflict. It hardly warned his bombers to spare the mosques of Isfahan.
Of international bodies, UNESCO is active in keeping a record of the fate of cultural heritage worldwide, but a record is just a record. Its listing of Russia’s and Israel’s devastation of their hated foes is like watching a historic tragedy unfold in real time. We might almost prefer it to happen behind our backs.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Photo: AP

Pancreatic cancer study shares findings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:45:47 UTC
01:45:47 KST

A study by researchers at the National Health Research Institutes (NHRI) found that having low levels of serum carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9), a pancreatic tumor biomarker, in people with pancreatic cancer does not necessarily indicate a better prognosis.
NHRI’s National Institute of Cancer Research assistant investigator and attending physician Su Yung-yeh (蘇勇曄) said pancreatic cancer is the seventh leading cause of cancer death in Taiwan, and about 80 percent of patients were diagnosed at an advanced stage, with five-year survival of only about 13.7 percent.
Doctors typically use CA19-9 levels to assess a person’s risk, helping them decide treatment options and monitor treatment response, he said, adding that CA19-9 (also known as Sialyl Lewis antigen A) is a tumor marker protein that can be measured through a blood test and is typically elevated in people with pancreatic cancer.
Photo: CNA
It is generally believed that higher levels of CA19-9 indicate more advanced disease and a worse prognosis, and that a value below 37 units per milliliter (U/ml) is considered normal, making it a key indicator, Su said.
However, about 10 percent of people with pancreatic cancer do not have elevated CA19-9 levels, even in cases of advanced disease, Su said.
These people’s low CA19-9 levels are actually influenced by genetics — genetic polymorphisms in the FUT3 genes — that impairs CA19-9 production, he said.
Doctors without access to people’s genotyping cannot distinguish Lewis antigen-negative people with advanced disease from those with genuinely low tumor burden.
To establish new CA19-9 thresholds for Lewis antigen-negative people and better predict their prognosis, the research team examined FUT2/FUT3 genetic variants in 615 people with pancreatic cancer at National Cheng Kung University Hospital and Kaohsiung Medical University Hospital in Taiwan.
They identified a CA19-9 level of 7U/ml or less as a new threshold for identifying people with pancreatic cancer who have the Lewis antigen-negative genotype, Su said.
The study also found that Lewis antigen-negative people with a CA19-9 level of 7U/ml or less experienced outcomes comparable to patients with CA19-9 levels of greater than 200 units/mL, he said.
Patients with CA19-9 levels of 7U/ml or less had a median overall survival of 13.5 months, similar to the median overall survival of 12.8 months seen in people with levels of more than 200U/ml, he said, adding that it suggested levels of 7U/ml or less might be prognostic of high-risk disease
In comparison, those with CA19-9 levels between 7U/ml and 37U/ml had a median overall survival of 23.2 months, while people with levels greater than 37U/ml to 200 units/mL had a median overall survival of 22 months, he added.
Su said that they suggest using a dual-threshold CA19-9 model with a cutoff of 7U/ml or less to identify high-risk Lewis antigen-negative patients, and improve their risk stratification and prevent underestimation of their disease severity.
The study was published in the journal Clinical Cancer Research in May, the NHRI said.

World No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka needed six match points to subdue Talia Gibson on Sunday and join reigning Grand Slam champions Elena Rybakina and Mirra Andreeva in the third round of the Cincinnati Masters.
Australia’s Gibson saved five match points in the 12th game of the second set before Sabalenka came through in the tiebreaker, managing to get the job done 6-2, 7-6 (7/2) in just under two hours on a windswept Grandstand Court.
“I’m super tired, this is crazy weather,” Sabalenka said. “Talia played great tennis and was more aggressive in the second set.”
Photo: AFP
“She put more pressure on my service games,” Sabalenka said. “I’m glad I stayed calm and pulled it out in straight sets.”
Sabalenka won Cincinnati in 2024 and is hoping for a deep run to carry her into the US Open, where she is seeking her first Grand Slam title of the year.
The Belarusian has won three titles in this year, but none since Miami in March.
She advanced along with Australian Open winner Rybakina and Roland Garros champion Andreeva, who powered on in convincing style.

“Today I’m happy with the serve,” she said. “Definitely it helped me a lot. Last week in Toronto was very difficult. A lot of three set matches.”

Gauff and Shelton headlined an evening session that proved tricky as blustery conditions gave way to brief rain that halted their matches for just under half an hour.
Gauff pulled out victory with a storming finish, winning the last five games.
Shelton fell victim to the same sort of surge from Faria, who rallied from 4-1 down in the second set to post his first top-10 win with a 6-4, 6-4 triumph over the American.
“These moments, you got to take it all in and just enjoy it,” Faria said. “It’s a very emotional moment for me and my team, to do it here in front of an amazing crowd and against the home player at night at an amazing venue just makes it a little more special.”

Taiwanese inventors win big at Silicon Valley festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:45:44 UTC
01:45:44 KST

Taiwanese inventors won big at this year’s Silicon Valley International Invention Festival (SVIIF) in California, taking the event’s top prize, 24 gold medals and other special awards.
The festival featured entries from more than 30 countries in two categories — general inventors and youth aged seven to 18 — and the awards included SVIIF’s first and second prizes, as well as special awards from partner organizations.
Taiwanese students who designed "AllerDetect GO" won the top prize in the Youth Talent Competition category, drawing cheers from the audience when the team went onstage to receive the honor on Sunday last week, final day of the three-day festival.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Invention Association via CNA
The "AllerDetect GO" app is a health protection system designed for children, older adults and people prone to allergies.
Combining detection, alert, record-keeping and smart home response functions, it helps users identify potential allergen risks earlier, reduces accidental exposure, and builds a safer day-to-day health protection system, the inventors said.
The second prize went to a team from the Affiliated Senior High School of National Taiwan Normal University.
In the general inventors category, Baichao Greenergy Tech Co won the special award from the World Intellectual Property Organization.
Kang Chiao International School’s 10-year-old Hsu Ting- wei (許庭維), who on Saturday won a gold medal at SWIIF for his "Novel Artificial Electronic Nose," also received the International Federation of Inventors’ Associations best invention award.
The invention is an intelligent, non-contact security screening platform that combines a real-time air sampling system, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and artificial intelligence-based odor recognition technology. It can be installed behind X-ray baggage screening equipment at locations such as airports.
Hsu did not receive the award simply as encouragement because of his age, but because the jury genuinely recognized his efforts and believed his invention had practical value and left a deep impression on the judges, jury chairman Amin Ghafooripour said.
Earlier on Saturday, Hsu said he hoped that his invention could help prevent pork products that might be carrying African swine fever from entering countries, as well as help the US stop drugs such as fentanyl at its borders.
Besides presenting special international awards, SVIIF handed out medals and certificates to participating inventors on Saturday, with entries receiving gold, silver or bronze medals.
Taiwanese inventors won a record 24 gold medals this year, along with eight silvers and one bronze from 35 entries across the general inventors and youth categories.
Matt Nuccio, a SVIIF board committee member, praised the young Taiwanese participants.
"Taiwan had quite a few great innovations," Nuccio said, adding that he was particularly impressed by the quality of their inventions given their young age.
Taiwanese inventors tended to focus on applying new technologies to develop practical solutions that could make everyday life easier for people, Ghafooripour said.
Nearly every Taiwanese team won an award, and the gold medal count was the highest for Taiwan since it first participated in the Silicon Valley International Inventions Festival in 2018.
The festival was held in the Santa Clara Convention Center in California from Friday to Sunday.

輕鬆華語GO: 七夕的故事 The Original Story Behind ‘Qixi’

對話 Dialogue
清清：最近好多餐廳都推出七夕套餐，連飲料店也有活動。
Qīngqing: Zuìjìn hǎo duō cāntīng dōu tuīchū Qīxī tàocān, lián yǐnliàodiàn yě yǒu huódòng.
PHOTO: Unsplash / 照片：Unsplash
華華：對啊，現在大家都把七夕當成華人的情人節。
Huáhua: Duì a, xiànzài dàjiā dōu bǎ Qīxī dàngchéng Huárén de Qíngrénjié.
清清：我一直以為七夕本來就是情人節，難道不是嗎？
Qīngqing: Wǒ yìzhí yǐwéi Qīxī běnlái jiù shì Qíngrénjié, nándào bú shì ma?
華華：其實不是。以前的人會在這一天向織女祈求心靈手巧，所以七夕又叫乞巧節。
Huáhua: Qíshí bú shì. Yǐqián de rén huì zài zhè yì tiān xiàng Zhīnǚ qíqiú xīnlíng shǒuqiǎo, suǒyǐ Qīxī yòu jiào Qǐqiǎo Jié.
清清：原來如此，那牛郎和織女的故事呢？
Qīngqing: Yuánlái rúcǐ, nà Niúláng hé Zhīnǚ de gùshì ne?
華華：後來大家把這個傳說和七夕結合，慢慢就變成現在熟悉的情人節了。
Huáhua: Hòulái dàjiā bǎ zhège chuánshuō hé Qīxī jiéhé, mànmàn jiù biàn chéng xiànzài shúxī de Qíngrénjié le.
清清：沒想到一個節日，背後還有這麼多故事。
Qīngqing: Méi xiǎngdào yí ge jiérì, bèihòu hái yǒu zhème duō gùshì.
華華：所以今年過七夕的時候，除了吃大餐，也可以跟朋友分享這個有趣的由來。
Huáhua: Suǒyǐ jīnnián guò Qīxī de shíhou, chúle chī dàcān, yě kěyǐ gēn péngyǒu fēnxiǎng zhège yǒuqù de yóulái.
翻譯 Translation
Qingqing: Lots of restaurants are offering Qixi set meals lately, and even drink shops have special promotions.
Huahua: That’s right. Nowadays, most people celebrate Qixi as Chinese Valentine’s Day.
Qingqing: I always thought Qixi had always been Valentine’s Day. Or am I wrong?
Huahua: Not exactly. In the past, people prayed to the Weaver Girl for wisdom and skillful hands, so Qixi was also known as the Qiqiao Festival.
Qingqing: I see. Then what about the story of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl?
Huahua: Later, that legend became closely associated with Qixi, and over time the festival came to be known as Chinese Valentine’s Day.
Qingqing: I had no idea there was so much history behind this festival.
Huahua: This year, besides enjoying a nice meal, you can also share its interesting origin story with your friends.

1. 七夕 (Qīxī) Qixi Festival
2. 套餐 (tàocān) set meal
3. 祈求 (qíqiú) pray for
4. 心靈手巧 (xīnlíng shǒuqiǎo) clever and skillful
5. 乞巧節 (Qǐqiǎo Jié) Qiqiao Festival
6. 傳說 (chuánshuō) legend
7. 熟悉 (shúxī) familiar
8. 由來 (yóulái) origin

Study highlights erroneous use of AI in academic articles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:45:40 UTC
01:45:40 KST

A report released yesterday found that 16.1 percent of references in Taiwanese academic articles are suspected to contain citation errors or artificial intelligence (AI) hallucinations, in which generative AI and large language models fabricate sources, references or citations.
The study examined academic integrity, scanning 26,635 references using the Paper Plagiarism Verify System, developed by the Doublemind AI education system.
The system found that traditional plagiarism, which is defined as more than 70 percent similarity to other published works, accounted for only 5.5 percent.
Photo: Reuters
Meanwhile, 16.1 percent of references were found to be incorrectly cited or were suspected to have been fabricated by AI, highlighting a new challenge for academia in the face of rapidly developing AI, it said.
A further 12.3 percent contained errors in factual claims that conflicted with publicly available evidence or had no supporting evidence at all, it found.
Previously, systems were scanning whether documents were plagiarized from other sources, but with the widespread use of AI, the challenge is now detecting whether the sources cited actually exist, and whether the information it includes is true, Doublemind CEO Lin Cheng-hong (林政宏) said.
In academic literature, fake citations could provide authors, publication dates, academic journals and even digital object identifier numbers — unique codes that identify research papers — for work that does not exist, he said.
Such fabrications can be difficult to detect with the naked eye, he added.
Doublemind would continue strengthening its verification tools while also holding a series of outreach lectures to promote education on academic ethics, he said.
The company hopes to work with universities and high schools to establish an objective, verifiable and rigorous environment of academic integrity, he added.

European stock markets closed mostly lower on Monday as rising government bond yields and continued geopolitical tensions outweighed support from a weaker US dollar and reduced expectations of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike.
The STOXX Europe 600, which represents around 90% of the market capitalization of developed European equity markets, fell 0.22% to 656.41 points.

The UK’s FTSE 100 decreased 0.28% to finish at 10,720.3 points.
Italy’s FTSE MIB bucked the broader negative trend, edging up 0.01% to 53,586.98.
Investors also assessed the outlook for US monetary policy following weaker-than-expected retail sales and labor-market figures, which reduced expectations that the Fed would raise interest rates again in the near term.
The dollar index fell to around 99.19, its lowest level in about 10 weeks, as markets scaled back their expectations for further US monetary tightening. Investors are now awaiting the minutes of the Fed’s July meeting for additional indications about the future path of interest rates.
The euro appreciated about 0.16% against the dollar, with the euro-dollar exchange rate trading around 1.1589.

Holy water: nuns fight Italian town’s plans to take away their beach club
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:44:10 UTC
01:44:10 KST

A group of Italian nuns is fighting back against local council plans to take their beach club away from them – the latest flashpoint in the long-running debate about the monopoly of private concessions along Italy’s coastline.
The dispute, described as “a holy war” by some local press, unfolded when a 50-metre stretch of sand at Bagni Gino Garrone, a beach resort in the Ligurian coastal town of Spotorno managed by nuns from the Suore di Carità di Santa Maria order, was designated for public bidding by authorities as they seek to comply with EU beach concession laws as well as regional regulations on free beach quotas.
The nuns have been managing the resort since 1946 after being exempt from standard commercial rules because they were using the proceeds for charitable purposes, including funding an infant school they still run in Spotorno and a summer beach camp.
For decades they have been renting out loungers and umbrellas, so operating much like thousands of other private beach concessions, the difference being – they claim – that the proceeds go to fund their charitable activities.
However, with the regulation governing beach use for social missions no longer existing, they were told by Spotorno’s mayor, Mattia Fiorini, that the concession would be reclassified as a “free equipped beach” and if they wanted to continue running it they would have to compete in a public tender.
During a public debate on the topic, Sister Miranda, a nun in her 80s, challenged Fiorini. “It’s ours,” she was quoted as saying by the Turin edition of Corriere della Sera. “Why does the municipality want to take away our beach? If they do, we won’t even be able to keep the school running.”
Operating it as a “free equipped beach”, meaning access is completely free and people can choose to pay a small sum to rent loungers and umbrellas if they wish, would be considerably less profitable, the nuns argued.
Fiorini said if they wanted to continue managing the concession “they must participate in the tender, like everyone else”. The tender is due to be issued in the autumn.
The mayor’s plan means Spotorno could be among the first municipalities in Italy to meet a 30 June 2027 deadline for the country to put its current private beach concessions out to public tender, as per the EU’s Bolkestein directive.
For two decades, successive Italian governments – under pressure from powerful beach concession owners fearful of losing the often lucrative business – have resisted the competition rules. Giorgia Meloni’s government was forced to agree to the deadline amid pressure from Brussels and domestic court rulings.

Alaba has confirmed he took out two bounceback loans and he is understood to now be repaying the loans, according to the Times. But the MP did not answer questions on why he tried to wind up Alaba Properties Ltd and whether his companies were eligible for loans.
In a statement, he said: “Like many businesses and entrepreneurs, I accessed financial support during the Covid-19 pandemic. I am wholeheartedly committed to ensuring that the liability is met in full. I’ve referred myself to the Labour party’s investigations process on the matter and I’ll cooperate fully.”

China’s home prices extend decline in July amid persistent property slump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
16:40:50 UTC
01:40:50 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
17 August 2026•Update: 17 August 2026
Home prices in China continued to decline in July as falling property investment and sluggish sales prolonged the downturn in the country’s real estate sector, official data showed Monday.
New and secondhand home prices fell year-on-year in most of the 70 large and medium-sized cities monitored by China’s National Bureau of Statistics.
Prices for new homes dropped 1.1% from a year earlier in the four first-tier cities of Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen.
They decreased 2.8% across 31 second-tier cities and 4.2% in 35 third-tier cities.
Shanghai, China’s most populous city, was the only first-tier city to record an annual increase, with new home prices rising 3%.
On a monthly basis, new home prices in first-tier cities fell 0.1%, ending a four-month recovery trend.
The downturn was more pronounced in the secondary market. Secondhand home prices declined 3.7% year-on-year in first-tier cities, 5.1% in second-tier cities and 5.8% in third-tier cities.
New home prices in China have fallen on an annual basis since April 2022 as the property sector struggles with weak demand, declining investment and financial difficulties among major developers.
The prolonged housing downturn has weighed on household confidence and the broader economy because the property sector has historically been a major driver of Chinese investment and growth.

According to Zaghroun's testimony, the incident began when a woman, notably dressed in pro-Palestinian attire including a keffiyeh and a Palestinian flag, began shouting "Free Palestine" at the group. Her actions, which Zaghroun described as rhythmic clapping and gesturing like a fan in a stadium, quickly mobilized a surrounding crowd.
Within minutes, the group was encircled by hundreds of people. The initial protests escalated into overt and aggressive antisemitic rhetoric. Zaghroun described the atmosphere as terrifying, stating, "For 40 minutes, hundreds of people humiliated us and spat on us. There was a huge crowd around us. We feared we would be murdered. It was very scary."
As Zaghroun recounted, the harassment continued with the crowd shouting various antisemitic and anti-Israel slogans, including "Baby killers," "Jews are not wanted here," "Zionists are not wanted here," "Death to Israel," and threats directed at Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. According to his account, some individuals within the crowd explicitly threatened, "We are going to kill Jews."
Assailants didn't care that group wasn't from Israel
Zaghroun stated that despite his attempts to de-escalate the situation by explaining in French that he and his companions were from France and not Israel, the assailants continued their abuse, appearing indifferent to the group's nationality.
Zaghroun noted that one member of the group, a member of Chabad wearing traditional Jewish clothing, including a long coat and a black kippah, served as a particularly visible target during the encounter.
Recognizing that they were in grave danger, Zaghroun said the group eventually split up in an attempt to escape the crowd's encirclement. They ultimately managed to flee to their hotel, with the mob pursuing them as far as the building's entrance, according to his testimony.
Zaghroun, a Parisian of Spanish-Tunisian descent, emphasized that the attack was motivated solely by their Jewish identity.
The incident has been noted by the Federation of Jewish Communities in Spain noted that if the accounts were confirmed, "this would be one of the most serious episodes of antisemitic harassment recorded in Barcelona in recent years."  Zaghroun has filed a formal complaint in France, and Spanish authorities have confirmed they are investigating the incident.

Somali army clashes with rebel forces for control of key city Baidoa
Somali forces repel rebel fighters in Baidoa after intense fighting involving explosives and dozens of casualties.
Somalia’s army has said it has driven opposition fighters out of Baidoa, the largest city in Somalia’s South West State, after hours of heavy fighting.
The clashes erupted before dawn on Monday, when fighters loyal to the state’s former president, Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen, attacked positions held by federal forces, the Defence Ministry said.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Why Mogadishu clashes are deepening Somalia’s political crisis again
- list 2 of 3Somalia declares order restored after two days of fighting in Mogadishu
- list 3 of 3Puntland forces seize government-held camp in Somalia’s Galkayo
The ministry added that the assailants used vehicles laden with explosives but were repelled after federal forces killed 30 attackers. It accused Laftagareen’s forces of fighting alongside the al-Qaeda-linked armed group al-Shabab.
Earlier, in a Facebook post, Laftagareen’s camp claimed that its forces had captured the city centre.
Al Jazeera’s Catherine Soi, reporting from Nairobi in Kenya, said local residents described intense fighting in the early hours of the morning.
“People were just waking up, starting their morning prayers, when they started hearing blasts, gunfire, heavy fire as well. We have been talking to people who live in Baidoa who say that some of their homes and buildings have been destroyed,” Soi said.
Residents told the AFP news agency that the clashes were the fiercest since the Somali army took control of the city in March. Doctors Without Borders, which runs facilities in Baidoa, told the agency that several casualties had reached its hospital and fighting had occurred on two fronts.
Baidoa lies about 245km (150 miles) northwest of the Somali capital Mogadishu and hosts hundreds of thousands of people displaced by war and climate events.
Laftagareen had led South West State for more than seven years when, in March, he severed ties with Mogadishu over controversial constitutional amendments pushed through by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud.
The changes extended Mohamud’s term in office by a year and drastically altered Somalia’s fragile power-sharing arrangement, enshrined in its 2012 provisional constitution.
The move sparked clashes across the nation, including in the capital, amid which the Somali army seized Baidoa, leading Laftagareen to resign.
Fighters loyal to him have struck the city repeatedly since, including a failed attempt to retake control of the state in May.
The clashes and instability are contributing to a severe humanitarian crisis in the country, where millions are facing malnutrition and famine.

Northern Ireland police arrest and charge a man in his 30s over the attack on i24NEWS
“This is not the Northern Ireland that I grew up in, the Northern Ireland that I’m still very proud to call home.”
A man in his 30s has been arrested and charged following an attack on an Israeli i24NEWS crew in Belfast, Northern Ireland, as concerns over antisemitism and hostility toward Israeli journalists continue to draw attention.
The suspect faces charges including assault occasioning actual bodily harm, common assault, assaulting a police officer and two counts of possessing an offensive weapon in a public place. The case is expected to be reviewed by Northern Ireland’s Public Prosecution Service, while the investigation remains ongoing.
The incident took place over the weekend as i24NEWS reporter Jonathan Roe and photographer Nadav Abs were filming a documentary series examining the rise of antisemitism in Europe. According to reports, the crew was interviewing people at a Belfast bar complex when a local man allegedly became aggressive after learning that they were an Israeli television crew.
The suspect reportedly attempted to take the crew’s camera equipment and continued to interfere with their work. When Roe and Abs tried to leave the area, he allegedly followed them and behaved threateningly. After the journalists sought assistance from nearby security personnel, the suspect allegedly threw a large glass beer mug at Abs from close range.
The glass struck the photographer in the head, leaving him with a bleeding injury. The crew later left the scene safely and did not require further medical treatment.
The attack has prompted renewed discussion about the atmosphere facing Israelis and Jews in parts of Europe.
Speaking to i24NEWS, David McIlveen, a former Northern Ireland legislator and founder of DUP Friends of Israel, strongly condemned the incident.
“This was a disgusting, despicable attack on three journalists,” McIlveen said. “This is not the Northern Ireland that I grew up in, the Northern Ireland that I’m still very proud to call home.”
McIlveen said he hoped the journalists would not allow the incident to define their experience of Northern Ireland.
“I hope that they will remember the good things that they saw in Northern Ireland and not be defining the place by this despicable attack,” he said.
At the same time, McIlveen acknowledged that antisemitism and hostility toward Israel are concerns that must be addressed. He argued that the current climate is influenced not only by Northern Ireland’s complicated history, but also by developments across Europe and the impact of social media.
“I think there’s a clear problem, but I believe it is an isolated problem,” he said, while stressing that Northern Ireland has its own experience with political violence that should inform how people respond to the conflict in the Middle East.
“Northern Ireland, of all places, knows the difference between a victim and a terrorist,” McIlveen said. “We’ve had to learn that the hard way.” “There are many, many more supporters for Israel than there would be in lots of other parts of the United Kingdom,” he said.
Addressing Israelis who may now feel increasingly uncomfortable or unsafe traveling in Europe, McIlveen acknowledged that incidents such as the Belfast attack can understandably fuel those concerns.
“First of all, I would say I get it. I understand,” he said. “Certainly when you see scenes like what happened in Belfast and what happened in other places, I completely understand why Israeli people may be feeling that way.”
But he urged Israelis not to allow isolated incidents to shape their entire perception of Northern Ireland.
“I can assure all of your viewers that certainly when it comes to Northern Ireland, it is an open, welcome place for everyone,” McIlveen said. “We support you 100%. And please do not be discouraged by a small group of people who are too blind to see the reality of what’s going on.”
Roe and Abs have since completed their work in Northern Ireland and returned safely to Israel. The Belfast incident is part of a wider i24NEWS documentary project examining the rise of antisemitism in Europe and beyond.

Russia has destroyed 14 stadiums in Ukraine since the beginning of the war

Russia has destroyed 14 stadiums in Ukraine since the beginning of the war
Kyiv • UNN
Since the beginning of the full-scale war, Russian occupiers have damaged or destroyed 88 stadiums in Ukraine, 14 of which have been completely destroyed. Direct losses to sports infrastructure are estimated at $4 billion.
Since the beginning of the war, Russian occupiers have damaged or destroyed 88 stadiums in Ukraine, 14 of which were completely destroyed. Direct damage caused to sports infrastructure is estimated at $4 billion, UNN writes.
Details
On Friday, August 7, Russia’s army attacked Odesa, damaging the Chornomorets football stadium. The attack damaged the roof, glazing, and stands. The stadium’s press service said that it was assessing the extent of the damage and determining the scope of work required for restoration.
It later became known that a significant part of the restoration work had already been completed, and the hotel, office, gym, conference rooms, and all facilities on the premises continued to operate as usual.
Cases such as the one involving Chornomorets Stadium are not isolated. In response to a request, the Ministry of Youth and Sports told UNN that since the beginning of the Russian Federation’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, damage to or destruction of 88 stadiums has been reported in total, including:
-  44 – damaged;  
-  30 – partially destroyed;  
-  14 – completely destroyed.  
Stadiums in 14 regions of Ukraine have suffered damage or destruction. The largest number of such facilities was affected in Kherson region – 18, Donetsk region – 17, Kharkiv region – 16, and Luhansk region – 9. In Zaporizhzhia region, 7 stadiums suffered damage and/or destruction; in Dnipropetrovsk and Kyiv regions – 5 each; in Sumy region – 3; in Chernihiv and Mykolaiv regions – 2 each; in Poltava, Odesa, and Khmelnytskyi regions – 1 each; as well as 1 stadium in the city of Kyiv.
The ministry reported that, according to the results of the fourth phase of the Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA4), conducted jointly with the World Bank, direct damage to Ukraine’s sports infrastructure as of December 2024 was estimated at approximately $374 million. At the same time, the RDNA5 report estimates direct damage to cultural, sports, and tourism infrastructure collectively at $4 billion, without separately identifying the sports component.
Stadiums destroyed at the beginning of the war
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Chernihiv, located near the Russian border, has remained under constant threat of enemy strikes. At the very beginning of the major war, specifically on March 5, 2022, Chernihiv’s main arena and the home stadium of Chernihiv’s Desna, which, incidentally, suspended its participation in the Premier League because of Russia’s aggression – Yuri Gagarin Stadium – was damaged during artillery shelling, with the occupiers striking the eastern stand.
Yuri Gagarin Stadium from above
The arena suffered its most destructive strike on the night of March 11, when Russian aircraft dropped 8 aerial bombs on the stadium grounds. One of the stands was then almost completely destroyed, the football pitch suffered significant damage, and the sports complex’s infrastructure was reduced to ruins. The explosions destroyed the spaces beneath the stands and damaged administrative buildings, utilities, and the surrounding area.
From the first days of the full-scale invasion on February 24, Mariupol was under constant shelling, resulting in the destruction of the vast majority of buildings. The city in Donetsk region, which was defended to the last by Azov fighters, has been under complete Russian occupation since May 20, 2022.
One of the structures damaged by shelling from Russian forces was the arena of the city’s main football team, FC Mariupol, which could accommodate more than 12,000 spectators.
As in the case of Desna, Mariupol also suspended its participation in football competitions because of Russia’s aggression. In 2022, Mariupol vice president Andrii Sanin posted a video and photographs of the destroyed stadium. The stadium had once hosted matches of the 2009 UEFA European Under-19 Championship, where our youth team won by defeating their English counterparts in the final (2–0). At that time, the English team included Kyle Walker, Danny Welbeck, Kieran Trippier, Danny Drinkwater, Andros Townsend, and other English stars.
Russians like to claim that they are rebuilding Mariupol, which they themselves destroyed, but the condition of the stadium can be seen even on Google Maps.

Attack on Dynamo Stadium
On May 24, on the eve of the final round of the Ukrainian Premier League, Kyiv experienced another massive attack involving strike UAVs, air-, sea- and land-based missiles, as well as the "Oreshnik", with which the Russians hit garages in Bila Tserkva.
As a result of the attack, more than 30 people were injured, including children. At the same time, Dynamo Valeriy Lobanovskyi Stadium was damaged by falling debris from downed enemy targets.
The blast wave and debris damaged the arena’s infrastructure: windows were blown out in the club office, the building’s facade was damaged, and tiles at the stadium’s main entrance were also damaged.
Fortunately, the stadium’s pitch and stands were not damaged, allowing Dynamo to play against Kudrivka in the UPL’s final round (3:2).

The games were supposed to begin several hours after the attack… and after the air raid alert was canceled, they began," Dynamo press officer Andriy Shakhov Jr. wrote on Instagram.
Polissya Stadium
In March this year, the home stadium of Zhytomyr’s Polissya was also damaged during the shelling of Zhytomyr. The strike occurred in the area between the VAR vehicle and Section 18, which is located near the ultras. The strike caused deformation of the metal fences, damage to the stand structures, and damage to some of the plastic seats.
Polissya managed to promptly organize restoration work, eliminate the consequences of the destruction, and even announce plans to complete the eastern and southern stands so that the stadium would acquire the features of a full-fledged arena with stands on all four sides.
"The permitting documentation is currently being resolved; we are cooperating and communicating with the owner—the regional council, which provides all the relevant permits for the lease of the land plot," Polissya General Director Volodymyr Zahurskyi said.
Attack on Vorskla’s Training Stadium
In January 2026, as a result of air defense operations and falling debris in the Poltava region, the roof of one of the enterprises and a sports field were damaged. The pitch at Molodizhnyi Stadium, where Vorskla’s senior and women’s teams held training sessions, was also damaged; earlier, Vorskla U19 had played its matches there as part of the youth championship.
Attacks on Kharkiv’s Stadiums
In July 2022, infrastructure at the city’s main stadium—Metalist Regional Sports Complex, where UPL matches are not held due to the security situation—was damaged as a result of another shelling of Kharkiv. At around five in the morning, the occupiers shelled a residential area near the Sportyvna and Zakhysnykiv Ukrainy metro stations, where the home arena of Kharkiv clubs Metalist and Metalist 1925 (now Kharkiv) is located. Explosions sent shrapnel across the stadium pitch, damaging it.
On March 26, 2025, the Russian army attacked Kharkiv, Sumy, and Dnipro. In particular, a football match was taking place near Metalist Regional Sports Complex in Kharkiv. The footballers who were on the field began fleeing it, while those who did not manage to do so dropped to the ground for safety.
However, Russia is waging war not only against large stadiums, but also against school ones. Thus, in May 2024, Russian occupiers struck a school stadium where children were playing at the time.
An 8-year-old girl and three boys aged 14, 14, and 15 were injured in the attack. One of the boys had his leg torn off.
Occupied Stadiums
What immediately comes to mind in a football context when Donetsk is mentioned? Of course, FC Shakhtar Donetsk and Donbas Arena—the first stadium in Eastern Europe designed and built in accordance with UEFA Category 4 standards. According to UEFA and FIFA accreditation, the structure meets the "elite" class.
After the "miners" left their native city, separatists began to "look after" the stadium. Who could have imagined that the stadium where American singer Rihanna performed in 2011 and which hosted home matches during UEFA Euro 2012 would fall into such a neglected state: the area around the stadium and the landscape park are becoming overgrown with weeds, there are no crowds or events, and the structure itself is gradually deteriorating due to a lack of proper maintenance, although the façade made of Donetsk glass is still recognizable from the outside.
Regular maintenance of the green areas and roses has stopped, the lawns have turned yellow, and the paths are empty.

Of the 253 detentions made across 14 states, 62 were in Uttar Pradesh; 52 in Haryana; 51 in Delhi; 44 in Punjab; 15 in Rajasthan; 8 in Maharashtra; 5 in Uttarakhand; three each in Karnataka, Gujarat and Bihar; and two each in Telangana, Himachal Pradesh, J&K and Kerala — with fresh FIRs registered in Delhi and Karnataka.

Indian security forces ripped apart the network by launching coordinated operations across different locations in 14 states, upholding (a) brilliant example of India's zero-tolerance towards terrorism".Shah added that the substantial recoveries made from the operatives of the ISI-funded group and their hideouts include IEDs, grenades bearing Pakistan Ordnance Factory markings, pistols, live cartridges and CCTV cameras used for espionage. "The network was involved in several terrorist activities," he shared.
MHA in a statement said that SBN is a Pakistani-based, ISI-backed syndicate linked to grenade, IED and petrol bomb attacks and targeted killings across India. It has also been paying local conduits to recce police, defence and religious sites, and to install CCTV cameras for espionage, added the ministry.Cumulatively, over 80 FIRs and 200-plus arrests have been recorded against SBN under UAPA, BNS, the Arms Act, NDPS Act and Explosive Substances Act. Recovery of grenades bearing Pakistan Ordnance Factory markings confirm the network’s direct cross-border links."Security agencies reaffirm govt of India’s zero tolerance for cross-border terror and continued coordinated action to dismantle SBN’s networks nationwide," said the home ministry.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012.
