College football rule changes include removing next-game DQs for a first targeting penalty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
15:53:02 UTC
00:53:02 KST

College football rule changes include removing next-game DQs for a first targeting penalty
Targeting penalties assessed in the second half of a game will no longer require the offending player to sit out the first half of his team’s next game, offensive pass interference will become a 10-yard penalty and the little-used fair catch kick will be introduced to college football.
Those are among the changes for the 2026 season, the National Football Foundation announced Tuesday in its annual summary of rules changes.
The targeting penalty change will be an experimental rule for 2026. A player disqualified for targeting for the first time in the season may participate in the following game. The trial rule will apply regardless of which half the targeting penalty is called.
A player who draws his second targeting penalty of the season will be required to miss the first half of the next game. A player who draws his third targeting of the season must sit out the full following game.
A conference can choose to initiate an appeals process after a player’s second targeting penalty. The appeal would be sent to the NCAA national coordinator of football officials for a video review. If the appeal is successful, the player would not be forced to sit out the first half of the following game.
Offensive PI now 10 yards
The penalty for offensive pass interference is being adjusted from 15 yards to 10 yards. The rules reserve 15-yard penalties primarily for personal fouls and unsportsmanlike conduct. Defensive pass interference will remain a spot foul, with a maximum of a 15-yard penalty.
Fair catch kick
In a change to align Division I rules with those in the NFL and high school, a team could choose to attempt a fair catch kick after a completed or awarded fair catch. The kick would be a place kick with a holder or a drop kick from the spot where the returner caught the ball. The defense would be at least 10 yards from the spot of the kick.
If the ensuing kick goes through the uprights, it would be worth three points.
The rarely used play last came up in the NFL in 2024 when the Los Angeles Chargers’ Cameron Dicker converted from 57 yards against the Denver Broncos.
Unsportsmanlike conduct
An automatic unsportsmanlike conduct penalty will be called if a player initiates any of these five actions or gestures: any act of simulating the brandishing of a weapon; slashing of the throat or a nose wipe signal; removing helmet after the ball is dead (with exceptions for timeouts and equipment adjustments); dead-ball contact fouls, such as pushing, shoving, striking, etc., that occur clearly after the ball is dead and that are not part of the game action; using forcible contact to push or pull an opponent off the pile after the ball is dead.
2 replay challenges
The head coach will now have two replay challenges per game. If a coach wins at least one of their first two challenges, they are awarded a third challenge. A challenge can be made only if the team has a timeout remaining and available; if the challenge is successful, the team’s timeout will not be charged.
Other changes
Coach-to-player communications through the helmet is now permissible for all NCAA divisions. ... Helmet attachments (e.g., Guardian Cap, SAFR Helmet Cover) that enhance player safety are allowed. All helmets, with or without the attachment, must be of the same color and design. ... Up to two sponsor patches are allowed on the jersey, with conference approval. A third patch is allowed in conference championship or postseason games. Logos may not exceed 4 square inches. One commercial logo, not to exceed 4 square inches, is permitted on the helmet.

Jets running back Breece Hall strains groin at practice. Tests planned, but Aaron Glenn optimistic
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. (AP) — New York Jets running back Breece Hall strained his groin during practice Monday and will have tests to determine the severity of the injury.
Coach Aaron Glenn appeared cautiously optimistic after practice that Hall’s injury wasn’t serious.
“I don’t think it was a big deal,” he said, “but I want to make sure I get the evaluation on that.”
Hall, the team’s top running back coming off his first 1,000-yard rushing season, caught a pass late in the practice session, pulled up and fell to the rain-slicked grass. He got up and walked gingerly to the sideline, where trainers appeared to be examining his upper right thigh/abdomen area.
“My stomach dropped a little bit, for sure,” backup running back Braelon Allen said. “From the sound of it, it don’t seem too serious, so hope we can get him back as quickly as possible.”
The 25-year-old Hall is considered a key to New York’s offense. He received a three-year contract extension in the offseason from the Jets worth up to $45.75 million. The team had used the franchise tag on Hall, whose contract — which will pay him $15.25 million per year — made him the third-highest paid running back in the NFL at the time.
Hall ran for a career-high 1,065 yards last season despite missing the final game with a knee ailment, becoming the first Jets player to top 1,000 yards rushing in a season since Chris Ivory in 2015. The 2022 second-round draft pick from Iowa State has 1,000 yards from scrimmage in three straight seasons, making him just the sixth player — and fifth running back — in franchise history to accomplish that feat.
If Hall needs to miss some time, the Jets’ backfield will be a bit short-handed. Isaiah Davis, a fifth-round pick in 2024, is sidelined with what Glenn has said is a minor knee injury. Allen, Kene Nwangwu and undrafted rookies Sam Scott and Chip Trayanum are the other running backs on New York’s roster.
“Injuries are a part of this league,” Glenn said. “It’s the biggest equalizer in this league. I think as a coach, obviously you don’t want to see any of your players go down, but you also have to continue to move forward.”
Allen, who was limited to four games with a knee injury last season, would step into the starter’s role if Hall is out for any practices and the two remaining preseason games. The 2024 fourth-rounder said it was a “sigh of relief” to run for a 31-yard touchdown in the preseason opener against Tampa Bay on Saturday night, showing he’s healthy.
“I know that most people think that, that once you lose a starter, there’s a huge drop-off,” Glenn said. “I like to look at it like all of our guys are starters.”
Geno Smith practices, but Garrett Wilson sits out with an illness
Quarterback Geno Smith was back on the practice field after sitting out the preseason opener with a sore ankle.
Smith wore a sleeve on his lower left leg and walked with a slight limp. He participated in team drills, but it’s uncertain if he’ll play in New York’s preseason game at Pittsburgh on Friday night.
Wide receiver Garrett Wilson didn’t practice because of a stomach illness, Glenn said.
Wilson caught two passes from rookie Cade Klubnik for 32 yards in one series in the preseason opener against Tampa Bay. Glenn said the star receiver came in and was vomiting Monday, but “he’ll be fine.”
Linebacker Mykal Walker injured a calf. Rookie cornerback Mory Bamba, who was one of the standouts against the Buccaneers with four passes defensed, has a knee injury that Glenn said will sideline him a few weeks.
Cornerback Qwan’tez Stiggers, who is in the concussion protocol after passing out during practice last week and briefly being hospitalized, was working in the rehabilitation area.
Linebacker Demario Davis and safety Minkah Fitzpatrick got the day off from practice for veteran rest days.
T’Vondre Sweat makes his training camp practice debut
Defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat practiced for the first time in training camp after being activated Saturday from the non-football injury list with a hamstring ailment.
Sweat was acquired from Tennessee during the offseason for edge rusher Jermaine Johnson. The 6-foot-4, 366-pound run-stuffing presence is expected to help anchor the defensive line. He was taken 38th overall by the Titans in 2024 out of Texas, and had three sacks and 85 total tackles in 29 games, including 28 starts, in Tennessee.
“Obviously, he’s a big man and he has the ability to take up two gaps,” Glenn said. “When you’re able to do that as a big man, it allows the linebackers to get a chance to run, and also he’s going to take up two blockers, which means, they’re missing a blocker on someone — that’s the reason why he’s here.”
Edge rusher Joseph Ossai also practiced after beginning camp on the physically unable to perform list.

PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — Lindsay Clancy’s mother and sister took the stand Monday to recount how they saw her become increasingly anxious, paranoid and suicidal in the months before she killed her three children.

Musgrove also recalled a more alarming disclosure in December, when she was standing in the kitchen with Clancy and her then-husband, Patrick Clancy. Musgrove said her daughter appeared nervous and told them she needed to tell them something.
“She told us she had thoughts of harming the children,” Musgrove said.
Musgrove, who lived in Connecticut, often stayed with her daughter in Massachusetts from October into December 2022. She said Clancy was scared of sleeping alone, became increasingly paranoid and believed the medications she was taking “were destroying her mind.”
Clancy’s sister described a similar decline. Allison Ozga testified that at the end of December Clancy told her she had experienced suicidal thoughts every day for a month.
The testimony came in the fourth week of Clancy’s murder trial, soon after the prosecution rested their case.
Prosecutors argue that Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, planned the Jan. 24, 2023, killings and contrived to get her husband out of the house by sending him to get takeout and to the pharmacy.
Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington does not dispute that she killed the children. But he says she shouldn’t be held criminally responsible because she had postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth. He said she also had bipolar disorder and that antidepressants prescribed worsened her condition.
‘How could a mother hurt her children?’
A former co-worker testified Monday about Clancy’s years as a labor and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, describing Clancy as a “really good” nurse who loved her job and was “compassionate, kind and a patient advocate.”
“She was the type of nurse that you wanted taking care of you or your loved one when you walked onto our unit,” said Margaret Hamp.
Hamp said she and Clancy worked night shifts together and that Clancy regularly sought parenting advice from her co-workers, asking about everything from children’s sleeping habits and choosing a daycare provider to monogrammed lunch boxes.
Hamp also recalled a conversation from Clancy’s first year on the unit after a pregnant patient arrived with plans to harm herself. Hamp said she spoke with Clancy about mental health during pregnancy and postpartum and asked whether she had heard of Andrea Yates, the Texas mother who drowned her five children in 2001.
“I explained that to her, and she cried,” Hamp testified. “She said, ‘How could a mother hurt her children?’”
A disputed picture of her mental health
Earlier in the trial, the jury heard that Clancy had sought treatment for severe mental health problems, including admitting herself to a psychiatric hospital. But witnesses also noted Clancy wouldn’t always take the medications prescribed to help with her insomnia, anxiety and depression, and that she expressed fears she was addicted to some of them.
The defense has argued that Clancy was overmedicated and that her care was disjointed, with doctors not speaking to one another or sharing notes. The defense also showed she was discharged from one facility after a day and denied a higher level of care at another when she couldn’t show that she had a suicide plan.
Prosecutors have questioned the seriousness of Clancy’s suicide attempt and showed through texts and photos that she performed many normal activities the day of the killings, including taking her children to the doctor and playing with them in the snow.
Her doctors have testified they never saw Clancy exhibit signs of mania or psychosis, though she did repeatedly talk of feeling suicidal.
Clancy hasn’t testified and isn’t required to do so, but jurors have seen her break down in sobs at several points, including when prosecutors showed the jury autopsy photos of the children.
At the start of the trial, Patrick Clancy described the horror of returning home to find his dead children. During his testimony, prosecutors played a harrowing seven-minute 911 call, which was not released to the public. Clancy can be heard checking on Lindsay Clancy in the backyard, before heading down to his basement and finding his children.
He screams and howls before telling a dispatcher, “She killed the kids!”

Imagining Ukraine's political system after the war
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
18:53:00 EEST
00:53:00 KST

Imagining Ukraine's political system after the war
Even if the terms of a ceasefire or peace settlement are satisfactory to most Ukrainians, the country's democracy will face its fair share of challenges.
Any projections about Ukraine's postwar politics should start with the recognition that Russia's ongoing war has taken the country into unknown territory.[1] It is possible to say that the war's scope and scale have had a social impact in Ukraine that can be compared only to that of a revolution. The war has dismantled the old social contract between the ruling elites and the people. Moreover, it has reshaped, if not redefined, the fundamentals of Ukrainian statehood. The war revealed the central role of civil society (including volunteer movements, grassroots mobilization, independent media, and influencers), exposed the strengths and weaknesses of state institutions and the legal system, and forced the Armed Forces and security services to adapt rapidly. However, to borrow Alexis de Tocqueville's phrase, no matter how profound the revolution, the new order inherits important traits and patterns of the old one.
The Long Shadow of Corruption
Populism and corruption have been formidable impediments to the economic and political development of independent Ukraine. In November 2020, the editorial board of the Financial Times opined on the constitutional and legal challenges facing President Volodymyr Zelensky in achieving his stated goal of dismantling the oligarchic state capture that had characterized Ukraine's political and economic system since independence in 1991. It expressed concerns that Zelensky, whom it called "a textbook populist," wanted to avoid an uphill struggle in tackling the roots of the problem, instead preferring quick solutions that enjoyed broad public approval.
After Zelensky was elected in 2019, he succeeded in converting his wide popular support into unprecedented control of the legislative and executive branches of government. During the first eighteen months of his presidency, terms such as "turbo regime" and "deoligarchization" reflected his almost unlimited power and the steamroller-like process he used to push new laws through parliament. He and his allies argued this was necessary to "reset" the political system and rid the country of entrenched oligarchic influence and high-level corruption.
However, it soon became apparent that members of Zelensky's entourage had taken over the existing schemes of illegal personal enrichment, even after the start of the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022. Since then, key figures of the executive have been investigated for corruption, including: the head of the Office of the President Andriy Yermak; three of his deputies (Oleg Tatarov, Rostyslav Shurma, and Kyrylo Tymoshenko); deputy prime minister Oleksii Chernyshov; former minister of defense and Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council Rustem Umerov; minister of justice and of energy Herman Halushchenko; and head of the State Property Fund of Ukraine, Dmytro Sennychenko. Some of the figures who faced charges—including Shurma, Sennychenko, and Timur Mindich, a businessman and the president's close friend—left the country days or hours before arrest warrants were issued, which infuriated the public because it showed that powerful figures could violate strict wartime border controls and had access to privileged information about investigations.
In addition, as of December 2025, fifteen members of parliament from Zelensky's Servant of the People party were being investigated for corruption, with some facing accusations of buying the votes of their colleagues. In January 2026, former prime minister Yuliya Tymoshenko, who leads a parliamentary faction that has aligned itself with Servant of the People, was caught red-handed by the National Anticorruption Bureau as she offered bribes to secure the votes of fellow members of parliament.
Already in 2023, one of the authors warned that Ukraine was backsliding in its fight against corruption and that the public would blame Zelensky and the government if the issue was not addressed. In a public opinion poll that year, 78 percent of respondents said that Zelensky was directly responsible for fighting corruption in the government and the military. Even though Ukrainians saw him as a national symbol of resistance against Russia, the implications of high-level corruption scandals were clear at the time: Unless the president took action against accused top members of his administration, perceptions of impunity risked undermining trust in him and damaging society's cohesion and will to resist the invasion.
The situation has grown worse since then. In a September 2025 poll, 71 percent of respondents—including 62 percent of those who said they trusted Zelensky—said that corruption had increased during the full-scale invasion. In an April 2026 poll, 54 percent of respondents said that corruption was a greater threat than military aggression, compared to only 39 percent who said the opposite.
These figures suggest that most Ukrainians see high-level corruption as a form of state treason and a threat to statehood. There is strong evidence that Zelensky, earlier in his presidency, was sensitive to such public attitudes; in 2023, for example, he publicly expressed a positive opinion about amending legislation to make the punishment for high-level corruption equivalent to that of state treason, which is a life sentence in most cases.
However, by 2025 popular outrage over corruption had turned against Zelensky. The clearest evidence of public anger about high-level corruption was the "cardboard Maidan" in July 2025—the wave of peaceful student protests against Zelensky's moves to curtail the powers and reduce the independence of anticorruption institutions in order to shield his allies from criminal investigation, including his longtime friend Mindich. It was a powerful reminder of the mass protests in 2004 and 2014 and showed that Ukrainians were willing to defy martial law,[2] which limits the constitutional right of peaceful assembly, in order to pressure the president on corruption.
Decentralized Resilience
Amid the invasion and malfunctioning state institutions, powerful civic activism, modern entrepreneurship, and the experience of decades of those who studied in the West went a long way toward enabling the national struggle for survival. Ukrainians' long tradition of solving problems in a decentralized manner when the central government was unwilling or unable proved critical to the country's resilience. Mayors and volunteers independently built ties with military units and used their resources to procure necessary lethal and nonlethal equipment needed on the front. Nongovernmental charity foundations like the Serhiy Prytula Foundation, the Come Back Alive Foundation, and the Sternenko Community led the way in providing millions of strike and reconnaissance drones, interceptor drones, electronic warfare systems, and access to commercial satellite imagery. These grassroots initiatives more than supplemented the state's resource-constrained and bureaucratically burdened efforts.
Moreover, the agility and adaptability of the defense forces were key factors that allowed Ukraine to survive in the initial phases of the full-scale war. This was the result of decentralized and self-organized networks of cooperation across broader sections of society. Just like community leaders and civic volunteers, the Army and National Guard brigades that turned out to be the most effective did not wait for plans to be introduced from the top. Rather, they independently established their own unmanned systems units, supply chains, research and development laboratories, medical infrastructure, training programs, and public-relations infrastructure.
These innovative practices reflect profound long-term shifts in the attitudes of Ukrainians, who have developed new expectations toward private initiative and state intervention, and have grown even more skeptical of relying on welfare provided by the government. This portends major shifts in postwar politics. Ukrainians will almost certainly continue to trust decentralized but well-connected networks of professionals at the national and regional levels more than they trust central government institutions or legacy political parties. Officers, volunteers, and entrepreneurs who made a difference during the war will have strong credentials for postwar leadership roles. Intense clashes are likely to emerge between wartime leaders and political figures viewed as products of the corrupt "old system." The victors in this competition will be those capable of mass mobilization through appeals to national security and justice, and who can build efficient nationwide political machines.
Zelensky's decision in mid-July to fire Mykhailo Fedorov, the tech-savvy minister of defense who is well-connected with top Western defense companies, illustrates this "clash of generations" in Ukrainian politics and governance. In his farewell statement, Fedorov outlined what he sees as major deficiencies in the "old way" of running the army and country during wartime. If Zelensky does not find a way to mend fences, Fedorov's dismissal might prove to be a watershed moment for old and new elites to consolidate and prepare for a postwar power struggle.
Moderates Versus Radicals
After the war, Ukraine will face the dual challenge of rebuilding while deterring new threats from Russia. The role of the state in recovery and development will grow significantly. This will require strengthening independent oversight and institutional checks and balances. It may also raise the issue of guaranteeing the welfare of all those working in the security and defense sector.
The public will expect the state to assist and support veterans, the relatives of fallen servicemen and civilians, former prisoners of war and deportees returning from Russia, and citizens who lost their homes and property because of hostilities. Debates over the extent to which the Ukrainian state should seek to hold Russian officials accountable for war crimes (if the international community fails to do so) and punish collaborators for their misdeeds are also likely to dominate the political landscape. Inevitably, there will be a national debate about the responsibility of Zelensky and the government for decisions made—or not made—before and during the war. Ukrainians will also demand close scrutiny of the activities of those who controlled politics and the economy before the invasion. These debates are likely to divide political actors and citizens into camps of "moderates" and "radicals," depending on whether they demand symbolic or uncompromising justice on key issues, and whether they favor selective or equal approaches to different actors and social groups.
The moderates camp will probably try to shift the focus away from immediate justice toward building a stronger state that is capable of protecting Ukraine and preventing a new attack. Figures such as Fedorov and Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov, who have consistently called for national unity and looked to the future rather than focusing on the past, might emerge as leaders of this camp. Moderates will try to direct public anger against Russia while seeking to defuse internal feuds. They will call for an acceleration of reforms necessary for joining the EU—which they will argue is the ultimate prize for postwar Ukraine and future generations. This camp will support special and "black" operations inside Russia and other countries to bring war criminals and traitors to justice.
Mobilization will be another issue that will divide Ukrainians after the war. Many thousands of men paid bribes to leave the country during the war or escaped mobilization by securing, through any means, exemptions from military service. At the same time, military commissions drafted thousands of unfit men, including with physical and mental disabilities, into service. These men cannot fight, but they also cannot be released from service until the end of the war, burdening the military and inflating the number of troops.
To address Ukraine's human-resources challenges, the moderate camp will probably call for the return of Ukrainians from abroad or argue in favor of migration from Africa, Asia, or Latin America to fill labor shortages. Moreover, to decrease public tensions over mobilization, moderates will argue in favor of increasing immigration and enrolling more foreigners in the ranks of the Armed Forces. (For instance, before his dismissal Fedorov was preparing a plan to substitute up to 50 percent of assault troops with contracted foreigners.) The idea is that such measures would encourage young Ukrainians not to leave the country because of the risk of being drafted to the frontline. In addition, Budanov has spoken out against mobilizing young Ukrainians, which in his view would threaten to eliminate an "entire generation."
However, the moderates will face a serious political dilemma. It will be hard to convince millions of refugees to return without strong security guarantees and economic stability, but it will be impossible to maintain a capable army and economic development in a situation of severe deficits of human resources.
The radicals will claim that any dilution of justice will lay the groundwork for another national disaster and a new Russian invasion. Their arguments may resemble those made in the early 1990s and in 2014, when certain political actors argued that all remnants of the old regime—whether former communists or collaborators of president Viktor Yanukovych and his Party of Regions—needed to be purged.
Several public figures with significant political and social influence—in the form of large followership in social media, the permanent attention of traditional media to what they say or do, and evident political ambitions—have the potential to become leaders of the radical camp. They are Serhiy Sternenko, a prominent volunteer and vocal opponent of Zelensky since 2021; Bohdan "Tavr" Krotevych, ex–chief of staff of the Azov Brigade; and Yuriy Butusov, former editor-in-chief of the Censor.net news portal and a drone company commander in the Khartiia Brigade. All three have attacked Zelensky for what they argue were poorly conceived and implemented decisions before and after the full-scale invasion.
Moreover, the radicals will call for the prosecution of political, administrative, and military leaders whose decisions contributed to Ukraine's devastation and huge human losses. Figures in this camp have already begun to criticize what they see as reckless, politically driven decisions that have cost the lives of thousands of the country's defenders with no operational or even tactical benefit on the battlefield. They have stressed the need for independent investigations of pointless offensive operations led by the assault regiments commanded by protégés of General Oleksandr Syrskyi, whom Zelensky removed as commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces in late July in response to public protests. They have also pointed out the absence of relevant basic military training for the majority of recruits in the Army. The public reaction to a recent independent investigation that uncovered the suspicious deaths of twenty-five recruits in the 425th Assault Regiment "Skelya" shows how sensitive and explosive this issue will become after the war.
Several whistleblowers, including decorated officers like ex-battalion commander of 46th Airborne Assault Brigade Colonel Anatoliy Kozel (Kupol), Major Oleksandr Shyrshyn from the elite 47th Mechanized Brigade, and ex-commander of 58th Mechanized Brigade Colonel Dmytro Kashchenko, have at different times warned about these and other critical shortcomings among senior political and military commanders. In April 2026, Colonel Roman Chervinskyi of the Security Service publicly accused Budanov of abusing power during the war.
These developments are alarming signs that after the war radicalized veterans and civic activists are going to shape the national agenda by saying that Zelensky and the executive failed to provide justice and security during the war. They will have a strong case to make if they can draw on the vivid memories of hardship felt by ordinary soldiers and their families.
Moreover, Zelensky himself has played a part in creating moderate and radical contenders. His dismissals of General Valeriy Zaluzhny from the position of commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces in 2024 and Fedorov in July were reminiscent of politics under former president Leonid Kuchma (1994–2004). Kuchma prosecuted moderate deputy prime minister Yulia Tymoshenko in 2000 and fired moderate prime minister Viktor Yushchenko in 2001. Both later came together to unite opposition forces and challenge Kuchma's regime during the election cycles of 2002–2004, culminating in the Orange Revolution and end of Kuchma's rule.
New Nationalism and Grassroots Structures
Two factors will determine whether the moderates or radicals win the support of the public and the postwar competition for power.
First, to be successful, political leaders and organizations will have to show that they embrace and practice a modern, sophisticated version of Ukrainian nationalism. The war proved to most Ukrainians that the nationalist political parties and groups who consistently warned about Russian threats and subversion in the fields of popular culture, education, and the economy had a point. The mainstream political establishment is already increasingly adopting elements of nationalistic ideology in its rhetoric. For instance, Zelensky in January 2026 issued an order to establish a "national pantheon" to commemorate the heroes of the fight for independence in the twentieth century, including leaders of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). In May, he announced the reburial of one of the OUN's leaders, Andriy Melnyk, and issued a decree renaming a unit of the special operations forces after the "heroes of the UPA." These decisions sparked a diplomatic crisis with Poland, which blames the OUN and UPA for Second World War atrocities against ethnic Poles. Many Ukrainians, however, see these organizations as having fought for Ukraine's independence against the Soviet Union, as well as against Nazi Germany.
At the same time, as one of the authors argued in 2022, Ukrainian nationalism has been transforming into a nonpartisan, inclusive civic ideology that is embraced by the majority. In a poll in March 2023, 65 and 47 percent of respondents, respectively, said they thought that new public figures such as Zelensky and Zaluzhny had played key roles in defending the country, demonstrating that Ukrainians see these two men as nation-building figures amid the horrors of war. In another 2023 poll, 42 percent named Zaluzhny as a symbol of Ukraine, second only to the poet Taras Shevchenko (56 percent). With 31 percent, Zelensky was ahead of the Second World War radical leader Stepan Bandera (27 percent), seventeenth-century Cossack hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky (26 percent), and Vyacheslav Chornovil, one of the leaders of the independence movement in the late Soviet period (26 percent).
The second factor is the importance of grassroots structures. Ukrainians have come to recognize the role of local communities, civic activists, and decentralized structures—especially military units—in building national identity. Popular units and leaders within them such as the Azov Brigade (Denys Prokopenko), the 3rd Assault Brigade (Andriy Biletsky), and the Khartiia Brigade (Oleh Kozhemyako) may become umbrella organizations for political movements. (Although its early roots were in far-right ideologies, Azov has the reputation of one of the most capable fighting units and one that cares about the lives of ordinary soldiers. It attracts volunteers from different age groups and gender, ethnic, and language backgrounds. Its commanders rarely take sides in political clashes.)
In sum, individuals who demonstrated leadership during the war and achieved military, technological, administrative, diplomatic, or humanitarian success will find themselves at the forefront of political competition after the war. The most successful postwar political forces will have strong national leaders with solid wartime credentials while relying on horizontal structures that emerged during the war, including volunteer networks, veterans groups, and informal associations of local community leaders.
In Search of a Unifying Figure
Amid public concerns over corruption and lingering questions about his wartime decisions, Zelensky's window of opportunity to be a national unifying figure has probably closed. But his political networks will give him a considerable opportunity to retain influence if he leaves office. Prior to his arrest in May 2026, Yermak—until then his closest aide—had launched a project to forge a coalition of military commanders, veterans, and volunteers with the goal of creating a new political force that could contest postwar elections under Zelensky's leadership. Since Yermak's arrest, Zelensky has continued this project on his own.
Zelensky has paid more attention to his standing and reputation among the military since he sacked Yermak in November 2025. Since the beginning of this year, he has participated in eight meetings with service members from various branches of the Armed Forces, suggesting that he is investing time and effort to rebuild support among veterans as a way to maintain political influence, whether he decides to run for another term or not.
On the other hand, former commander-in-chief Zaluzhny, now the ambassador to the United Kingdom, has emerged in the public consciousness as a strong contender for the presidency even though he has not yet declared his ambitions to run for office. He is a unique figure and is trusted both by moderates, who laud him for leading and modernizing the Armed Forces, and by radicals, who believe he is too strong to be subdued or corrupted by shadowy politics. At the same time, Zaluzhny is a political novice, and his knowledge of English and understanding of the economy, in particular, are significant shortcomings. He will have to prove to Ukrainians that he has the qualities to lead the country on the international stage through a turbulent postwar future.
Someone else may still yet emerge as a unifying figure. Ukraine needs its next leader not only to focus on healing a wounded nation, defending against Russian threats, and modernizing the economy, but also to unite political forces: If the first postwar president is accepted by moderates but not trusted by radicals, there is a high risk of dangerous civil division that will undermine medium- to long-term stability.
The Tough Task Ahead
On many occasions throughout its contemporary history, Ukraine has witnessed the emergence of new faces and new political forces. However, few of them survived the test of parliamentary democracy, especially when it came to coalition-building. Many leaders focused on their personal ambitions and created weak party structures that rose and fell in parallel with their own fate. Stronger political actors have tended to concentrate, if not monopolize, power in their hands at the expense of junior partners, and in some cases they went so far as to prosecute the opposition. Moreover, external influence, especially from Russia, has repeatedly turned heated domestic political competition into an existential fight. These factors remain and will frame postwar politics. Even if the terms of a ceasefire or peace settlement are satisfactory to most Ukrainians, the country's democracy will face its fair share of challenges.
Considering how bitter internal feuds undermined Ukrainian statehood in the past, Ukraine's key power brokers—including Zelensky, Zaluzhny, Budanov, Biletsky, and Prokopenko—should reach an agreement so that free and fair elections can be held across the country and then negotiate some form of power-sharing. Since all of them have armed men and women behind them, maintaining calm and ensuring that the next electoral cycle can proceed without voter intimidation will be critical. Ukraine has already seen in 1918–1921 a period of otamanshchyna, when anarchy and bitter power struggles between rebel warlords contributed to Ukraine being subjugated by Russia under Bolshevik rule. This time, Ukrainians must find a way to avoid bringing violence into the political process. It is vital that postwar election results be accepted and that power be peacefully transferred to the winners.
Ukraine's postwar leaders will have to decide how to reconcile national priorities—especially spending on defense and social welfare—with the demands of major donors like the International Monetary Fund and the EU, including those regarding democratic rights and the rule of law. They will also need to adapt domestic policies to the permanent threat from Russia without returning to martial law and without concentrating power under the executive.
So long as Ukraine is not a member of NATO or the EU, its leaders will have to build an agile and innovative national security architecture based on defense alliances and arrangements with other democracies, not only in Europe but also in the Middle East (Israel) and the Asia-Pacific (Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and the Philippines). Postwar Ukraine might also embark on trying to reshape its neighborhood. Ukrainians will have a hard time feeling secure with neighboring Belarus under the puppet regime of Aleksander Lukashenko and with Moldova's Transnistria region still a Russian-controlled enclave. Once the war ends, or even pauses, Ukraine's leaders are likely to address these threats, ideally in collaboration with the West but potentially unilaterally. They will need a more expansive and sophisticated view of engaging with countries in Africa, Latin America, and elsewhere. Its new leaders will need to maintain an equal focus on national defense and on securing the economic resources and trade relationships necessary to mitigate domestic demographic decline and fuel reconstruction.
These challenges will require the emerging crop of leaders to display a high degree of statesmanship. They must understand that personality-driven politics, polarization, legislative gridlock, and failure to respect the rule of law were profound mistakes that almost cost Ukraine its independence and statehood. If the country is to win the peace, it will need leaders who can break from the past once and for all.
Petro Burkovskyi, executive director of the Ilko Kucheriv Democratic Initiatives Foundation.
Olexiy Haran, is a professor at the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.

Russia’s Supreme Court upholds ban on anti-war party Yabloko
Russia’s Supreme Court on Monday upheld the exclusion of liberal opposition party Yabloko from September’s legislative elections, eliminating the country’s only explicitly anti-war party from the ballot, as dozens of the party's supporters were detained outside the court. The decision comes amid a wider crackdown on critics of Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
Russia's Supreme Court on Monday upheld its decision to bar Russia's only anti-war party, Yabloko, from running in the September legislative elections, as dozens of party supporters were detained outside the court.
Last week, the court removed Yabloko from the ballot, upholding a suit brought by a nationalist party, which blasted the rival for its peace stance and accused it of receiving foreign funding and copyright violations.
"The Appeals Chamber of the Supreme Court upheld the court's decision to revoke the registration of Yabloko's federal list of candidates for the State Duma elections," the party said in a statement, adding that it would seek a supervisory review.
During the hearing, police pushed the supporters away from the building, along with journalists who had come to cover the decision, including an AFP reporter.
"Many detainees today. We also see that the police officers are very nervous today," Kirill Goncharov, head of Yabloko's Moscow branch, told the independent outlet Novaya Gazeta.
Read moreAnti-war politician and Kremlin critic Boris Nadezhdin flees Russia for France
He earlier estimated that more than 60 party supporters had been taken to nearby police stations. Some teenage detainees had already been released, according to Goncharov.
In the courtroom, party leader Nikolay Rybakov called the detentions "intimidation".
The ban strips voters opposed to the four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine of their last option on the ballot.
Yevgeny Lyapin, who was outside the court, told AFP he had come simply to "support what is left of a declining democracy".
"I am neither a member nor a supporter of Yabloko, but I know that what is happening today is a blow to democracy across the whole country," he said.
Maria, 18, who came to support the party, said: "The president wants a great country; he talks about it all the time, and we want a free one."
In a separate case, Yabloko deputy chairman Lev Shlosberg was sentenced on Monday to 11 years and one month in prison over comments criticising Moscow's offensive in Ukraine.
With most of President Vladimir Putin's opponents jailed, in exile or dead, Yabloko is the only liberal party still operating in Russia.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

The justices rejected Trump’s request to revisit their June decision declining to hear his appeal of a 2023 jury verdict stemming from Carroll’s allegation that he sexually assaulted her in a Manhattan department store dressing room in the 1990s.

Feature: Is Ceuta's "Springboard Beach" really springboard?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
23:51:16 CST
00:51:16 KST

ALGECIRAS, Spain, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- On a beach near the border between Spain and Morocco, Reda and Mohcin were building what they called a house.
The two Moroccan men tied reeds together to form a frame, then covered it with plastic sheets and other materials they found nearby. Around them, dozens of similar shelters stood across the sand.
The beach is called Playa del Trampolin, the Spanish word for "Springboard Beach."
For many of those who reached Ceuta during the mass crossing from Morocco on July 30 and 31, the name appeared to carry a promise. This Spanish enclave on the North African coast could become a springboard to mainland Spain or another European country.
More than two weeks later, that promise remained uncertain. Different people on the beach gave different reasons for coming to Europe.
For Mohcin, the decision was closely connected to the future he imagined for his children.
He said cannabis use among young Moroccans was becoming increasingly common. He did not want the next generation of his family to grow up in such an environment. Furthermore, he hoped to find a safer and healthier life, with a chance to escape poverty.
When asked which country he wanted to reach, Mohcin did not name one. "It is up to fate," he pointed toward sky and said. "Anywhere is better than where I came from."
Reda believed his skills could give him a chance to establish a new life in Europe. He speaks English and French and described himself as someone prepared to work rather than depend on assistance.
He said many of those who had already returned to Morocco had crossed the border without a clear plan. "Most of those who went back were uninformed teenagers. They came just to join in the excitement," he said. "Those of us who have skills and genuinely want to change our lives have chosen to stay."
Nearby, Hamdi, a Tunisian who had lived on the beach for 17 days, operated a small stall selling snacks and cigarettes. He occasionally took food from his stock and gave it to younger migrants for free.
Hamdi said he was a plumber who could also install and repair air-conditioning systems. "I want to find a way to go to Madrid and work," he said.
For Kenza Lamchannek, family connections helped shape the destination she had in mind. She has a cousin in France and hopes eventually to reach the country.
Their reasons for leaving were personal: work, poverty, family, safety and concern for the next generation. Europe represented different things to each of them. None had a clear legal route to the destination they imagined.
During the interview, Reda's phone was running out of power. He asked the Xinhua reporter if he could borrow a power bank.
The reporter handed it to him and said it could be collected after another round of interviews on the beach. Reda appeared surprised and repeatedly expressed gratitude for the trust placed in him.
The small exchange revealed a wider distance between the people living on the beach and many of those who came to report on them.
Several migrants actively approached European media crews and asked to tell their stories. Kenza was among those eager to speak. She moved easily between four languages, explaining how she reached Ceuta, why she had hidden from police and where she hoped to go next. With her, language presented no obstacle.
The migrants remained highly visible to cameras across the beach. Their own voices were heard less often.
Their willingness to talk did not make their entry into Ceuta any less irregular. But it did show something else: the thousands described collectively as "migrants" carried different backgrounds, abilities and expectations.
Ceuta is Spanish territory and operates under a special border regime. Reaching the enclave does not automatically allow a person to travel onward to mainland Spain or another European country.
Spanish authorities have put the number of people who crossed into Ceuta during the July 30-31 surge at around 80,000. Many have since returned to Morocco, while an unclear number remain in the city awaiting identification, asylum decisions or other procedures.
The uncertainty has gradually transformed Trampolin Beach into a temporary settlement.
Each additional shelter makes the settlement more permanent, even as those building it continues to speak of leaving.
Reda and Mohcin do not know whether they will eventually travel onward or be returned to Morocco. For now, the immediate task is to finish the shelter.
At the end of the interview, they continued fastening materials to its frame.
On a beach named for a leap forward, they were building for an indefinite wait. ■

NEW DELHI, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- India's chief economic adviser V Anantha Nageswaran has proposed bringing back lower-ethanol-blend petrol for older vehicles, while allowing newer vehicles to continue using E20.
The suggestion came at a time when the Indian government had made E20, or petrol blended with 20 percent ethanol, the standard petrol blend nationwide.
In an op-ed published Monday in the New Delhi-based newspaper The Indian Express, Nageswaran and co-author Akash Poojari, a consultant in India's Department of Economic Affairs, proposed giving owners of older vehicles the option of buying E10, while newer vehicles continue to use E20.
According to the article, India has around 75-80 million two-wheelers built for E10, and many of these vehicles were not designed to run on higher ethanol blends.
The issue, they argued, is not simply about mileage. Older engines can face compatibility problems because ethanol can affect components such as rubber seals and fuel-system parts. Carburettor-based vehicles can also struggle with higher ethanol blends.
India rolled out E20 petrol last year, and since April 1 this year, it has been the only fuel available for sale at gas stations across the country. The move by the government is part of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's plans to reduce oil imports and help curb pollution. The government promotes it as a means to create a domestic market for ethanol produced from sugarcane, maize and other feedstocks. ■

Hundreds of Palestinians have returned to the Jerusalem Festival as the cultural celebration resumed after a three-year hiatus shaped by Israel's devastating war in Gaza.
The event, which will run for two months, opened on Sunday with a tribute to the late Lebanese musician Ziad Rahbani, a staunch supporter of the Palestinian cause.
At Yabous Cultural Centre, in the Israeli-annexed east of the city, the Jerusalem Arabic Music Ensemble played a selection of Rahbani's work.
"An evening dedicated to Ziad Rahbani represents a major part of our memory. Jerusalem needs this kind of event," filmmaker Yousef al-Salhi told AFP.
The Lebanese musician and playwright, the son of iconic singer Fairuz and a musical pioneer in his own right, died last year aged 69.
Throughout the evening, Rahbani's repertoire, from mawwal – slow Arabic free-form vocal music – to lively Levantine folk-pop, enthused the audience.
The last edition of the festival was held in the summer of 2023, before Israel's genocidal war in the Gaza Strip erupted following Hamas's Oct. 7 attack.
"We insist on coming back... Today we return to give people hope. The festival brings hope and brings people together," said musician Suheil Khoury, chairman of the board of the Yabous Cultural Centre.
The festival is now four decades old, though the city's tumultuous past means this is only the 30th edition, with several wars as well as the intifadas, or Palestinian uprisings, of the 1980, 90s and 2000s forcing it to pause.
The festival will continue with musical performances, cultural talks and art exhibitions taking place at various locations across east Jerusalem until Oct. 15.
"Everyone is thirsty for this kind of gathering amid the difficult circumstances we are going through – the genocidal war, restrictions on Jerusalem and the West Bank, and the violence being perpetrated against us," Mona al-Dajani, an academic researcher who attended the opening, said.
Moussa al-Qawasmi, a resident of east Jerusalem, was enthusiastic to attend an event promoting Palestinian culture.
"They (Israel) don't want us to exist, but no, we are always ready... we will continue to celebrate, sing and dance."

Supporting young people so they don’t become Neets | Letters

00:42:32 KST

Daisy Christodoulou suggests that teachers identifying children at risk of ending up not in education, employment or training (Neets) is like dentists helping children to learn to read (Could you predict which children will be Neets? No – and it’s unfair to ask that of teachers, 11 August). But dentists often help children learn to read by stopping the toothache that can derail education. Alan Milburn is not asking teachers to fix teeth. He wants the whole system to act when teachers identify barriers to learning.
We conducted the research at the centre of this debate. Our study showed that children identified with developmental difficulties through the statutory early years foundation stage profile (EYFSP) school assessment are much more likely to become Neets in late adolescence. The EYFSP reveals the holistic educational needs of children – but teachers cannot diagnose autism, treat anxiety or fix housing. Milburn is not making teachers responsible for everything.
Christodoulou is right that schools cannot eliminate poverty, repair the housing market or create jobs. But suggesting that we must separate children struggling at school from efforts to build our economy makes no sense. The tragedy of the rise in the number of Neets is that government acts by attaching an administrative label at the end of the journey through childhood. The research shows that there are warning signs years earlier when intervention is effective.
Our Child of the North and Centre for Young Lives campaign has consistently argued that children’s lives do not respect Whitehall boundaries. Health, education, social care and economic policy converge. Building a country that works for all children and young people is not the job of teachers alone. It’s everyone’s – including dentists.
Mark Mon-Williams
Professor of cognitive psychology, University of Leeds
I beg to differ with Daisy Christodoulou. It seems to me that good primary school teachers are more than adept at doing exactly what she is asking. My wife, starting her career in the slums of Newcastle and then in Wythenshawe, seemed to me to have an acute sense of the future that faced some children.
It might have been encouraged when, years ago, on a supply posting in a secondary school in the mining valleys of Wales, she asked an exasperating teenager what he expected to do when he grew up: “A policeman, ’cos I’ve got big feet.”
One thing she does know from bitter experience is the extent of Ofsted’s baleful influence on the role of teachers, especially in primary, in nurturing children. This was reinforced recently when a secondary school-trained Ofsted inspector effectively terminated the career of a much-loved and respected primary headteacher of our acquaintance after years of steady progress in a very difficult community. Let teachers get on with the job and give them the resources to do it.
Neil Blackshaw
Alnwick, Northumberland
 Daisy Christodoulou’s response is fair. Primary teachers have enough to do without speculating on children’s futures. Providing measured evidence on current strengths and weaknesses should be enough for secondary schools and services like careers guidance to support planning strategies for career development. Secondary schools are best placed to assess short and long-term potential, but they also need better training and structures to make this happen.
Simon Surtees
London

Battered by war, Iran’s rulers wary of more economic pain and unrest if US tightens pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
15:41:21 UTC
00:41:21 KST

Battered by war, Iran’s rulers wary of more economic pain and unrest if US tightens pressure
DUBAI - Even as Iran projects resilience in the war with the United States, its leaders are worried that a threat of more economic punishment by Donald Trump could increase hardships, reignite unrest and further erode the Islamic Republic’s legitimacy.
The US president vowed on Aug 14 to hit Iran hard economically, a day after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington would impose measures on Tehran that have "never been seen" as early as next week. Washington has not said what those measures will entail.
For all the bravado of Iran's leaders after holding out in nearly six months of conflict and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global oil supply route, they face mounting pressure at home that could result in nationwide unrest, according to three Iranian officials.
The officials, two political insiders, a former Iranian official and a dozen ordinary Iranians spoke to Reuters for this story on condition of anonymity, either for fear of retribution or because they are not authorised to speak to media.
Iran entered the war with high inflation, a weakening currency, energy shortages, sanctions and deep structural weaknesses, and must now contend with damaged infrastructure, disrupted trade, lost production and the cost of rebuilding.
Arshia, a civil engineer, spent a decade working in Iran’s construction industry before the war that began with the US and Israeli attacks on Feb 28 brought projects largely to a standstill.
He is now struggling to find work as projects are delayed or cancelled and costs soar, with little prospect of a rapid recovery.
“I’m worried. If Trump imposes more sanctions, how will ordinary people survive? I don’t want my country to be punished militarily or economically. We’re already struggling,” said the father of two from the central city of Isfahan.
His plight reflects a broader reality across Iran, where US strikes damaged factories, power plants, transport networks and other critical infrastructure, adding to pressure on an already strained economy.
Mohsen, 53, was forced to shut his small import-export business with Gulf countries after Iran retaliated against US strikes by targeting American bases and assets in the region.
“I had to lay off 10 employees. It was painful, but I had no choice. I could no longer afford to pay their salaries, and now I’m relying on my savings to support my family,” he said from the southern port city of Bandar Abbas.
Inflation, uncertainty hit households
Iran’s annual inflation rate reached 66 per cent in July, while consumer prices were 87.9 per cent higher than a year earlier, according to Iran’s Statistical Centre. Food inflation hit 128 per cent year-on-year.
For Iran’s rulers, the greater threat may be not economic pain itself, but the risk that worsening hardship reignites mass unrest, said the two insiders and one official.
The appointment of Hossein Taeb last week, a key architect of past crackdowns, to lead Iran’s Basij militia is one of the clearest signs yet of growing concern over a resurgence of unrest, a former reformist official said.
The Basij, a paramilitary volunteer militia, is affiliated with Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guards, which have both been used by the clerical rulers to quell protests.
Economic grievances have repeatedly spilled into nationwide protests in Iran in recent years.
In January, nationwide protests over economic hardships were crushed by the IRGC and the Basij force, with thousands killed.
In recent months, Iran’s clerical rulers have responded to fears of renewed unrest with executions, arrests, summonses and lengthy prison sentences targeting journalists, lawyers, activists, human rights advocates and students, rights groups say.
Officials say the measures are needed to maintain stability during wartime. Critics say they could deepen the divide between the clerical establishment and a public frustrated by rising economic pressures.
Salary ‘gone within days’
Families are cutting back on meat and other staples, opting for cheaper alternatives.
“I’m ashamed in front of my children. My salary is gone within days. Meat and chicken have disappeared from our table. I have no idea how we’re going to get by,” said Hossein, a government employee in the central city of Yazd.
Rents rose 31 per cent year-on-year in March, according to the Statistical Centre, while state media reported Tehran housing prices at roughly 50 per cent above 2025.
Iran’s minimum wage was raised by about 60 per cent in 2026, but continued rial depreciation has eroded purchasing power, with the dollar value of the minimum wage falling from about US$105 to US$86 (S$134-S$110) since late March.
Bijan, 40, earned about US$1,000 a month as an engineer when he entered the job market 15 years ago. He has since turned to online tutoring to make ends meet. Now, he and his wife struggle to make about US$400 a month and have left Tehran for a cheaper province.
“I used to work maybe five or six hours a day … Now, it’s all work or looking for work, or feeling anxious about not having enough work,” said Bijan.
For many Iranians, fear of renewed conflict has made planning for the future increasingly difficult.
US naval blockade ratchets up costs
Iran has sought to keep essential goods moving through alternative routes, including land corridors and the Caspian Sea, but those alternatives are also coming under strain.
Strikes on bridges have disrupted overland transport, increasing the cost and time needed to move goods into Iran.
President Masoud Pezeshkian last week acknowledged the squeeze, saying: “Our problems have multiplied several times over, while our income has also fallen.”
Goods that once arrived by ship now take longer routes into Iran, driving up prices, he said, adding that Iran is selling less oil and collecting less tax revenue from damaged or struggling businesses.
The blockade has also effectively cut off Iran’s petrol imports, lawmaker Reza Sepahvand told Iran’s ILNA news agency on Aug 15, adding that Iran’s daily petrol output had reached its limit at about 130 million litres, compared with consumption of 137 million litres. REUTERS

The national scheme of delegation, due to come into force on 31 October, will take away the ability from council leaders and planning committees to determine most planning applications, including the change of use proposed here. China’s economy showing signs that slowdown may be extending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
15:36:25 UTC
00:36:25 KST

China’s economy is showing signs of extending a slowdown with a slump in industrial output and retail sales in July, adding to pressure on Beijing to intervene with measures to support activity.
After the world’s second largest economy posted one of its lowest quarterly growth readings on record in the three months to June, the latest figures suggest it continued to falter in July.
Factory output grew 4.5% from a year earlier last month, compared with 5.3% in June, official figures from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed on Monday, missing a Reuters poll forecast for 4.8% growth.
Separate figures showed retail sales grew 0.6%, a slowdown from a 1% rise in June despite summer holiday tourism spending. Forecasters had predicted 1.5%.
The NBS said extreme weather, including high temperatures and heavy rainfall, had disrupted market supply and demand.
The latest snapshot, however is likely to increase pressure on policymakers to accelerate plans for tax and spending measures to support activity.
China’s premier, Li Qiang, suggested on Monday that efforts to bolster overseas demand for goods could be used to make up for weak domestic demand.
“Currently, the problem of insufficient domestic demand remains prominent, some industries and enterprises are facing increasing difficulties, and uncertainties in external environment are rising,” Li told a meeting of China’s state council, according to the state news agency, Xinhua.
“We should actively stabilise external demand, expand mutually beneficial international economic and trade cooperation and promote balanced trade development.”
Analysts say they expect stronger growth rates later this year, supported by spending measures from Beijing to increase activity.
“The silver lining is that the boost to manufacturing activity from AI capex [capital expenditure] continued to build, and that the wider weakness partly reflects temporary disruptions from recent typhoons,” said Julian Evans-Pritchard, the head of China economics at the consultancy Capital Economics.
“We still expect a modest uptick in growth over the rest of the year, supported by fiscal loosening.”
The latest snapshot comes after China posted a worse-than-expected annualised growth rate of 4.3% in the three months to June, one of its lowest quarterly readings on record.
The rate, which came in under the government’s target of 4.5% to 5%, was one of the weakest since Beijing began reporting official quarterly GDP data in the early 1990s.

Kushner, Israeli PM reportedly agree on path forward for Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
15:33:00 UTC
00:33:00 KST

Talks between the U.S. President Donald Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner and Israeli and Hamas leaders over the plan to end the war in Gaza concluded with no major breakthrough and he left Jerusalem on Monday, with both sides mainly standing firm on key demands.
Kushner met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a day after meeting the political leader of Hamas in Egypt in a bid to revive the plan.
Israel has carried out air strikes and seized more territory in Gaza despite an October cease-fire.
Kushner described his nearly four-hour meeting with Netanyahu as "good." Kushner added that Hamas representatives said "all the right things."
He also said that disarmament of Hamas could begin within 30 days.
"We could be seeing progress, you know, in as little as 30 days, hopefully on starting to take some of the weapons out and hopefully, you know, filling in some of the tunnels as well in the next 60 to 90 days as well," Kushner told Fox News.
Trump last month announced that Hamas had agreed to lay down its arms in phases, under a 15-point road map put forward by his Board of Peace to advance his plan, as Israel's military withdraws from Gaza.
Hamas said it agreed to the road map but implementation depends on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including halting attacks and withdrawing.
Netanyahu, whose ruling coalition is trailing in opinion polls ahead of an October national election, rejected the deal this month, insisting that Israel would not pull back until Hamas is completely disarmed.
There is a lot at stake, including the lives of some 2 million Palestinians in Gaza, reconstruction of the war-demolished enclave and future control over it.
Hamas says it has agreed to the road map, which includes disarmament, and the group is urging mediators and the U.S.-created Board of Peace to “compel” Israel to sign on.
But Israel, which under the road map must gradually withdraw from Gaza, says Hamas must fully disarm before any withdrawal.
Former British Prime Minister Tony Blair and Board of Peace Director Nickolay Mladenov were also in the meeting with Netanyahu, according to a source familiar with the plans and a diplomatic source.
Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting.
Netanyahu’s office said in a statement that he and the board had agreed to establish two working groups — one on the disarmament and demilitarization of Gaza and another focused on public health issues for Gaza.
Israel and the board agreed that the demilitarization “should be prompt and completed before any reconstruction,” the statement said.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister whose job is on the line in the Oct. 27 elections, has increasingly been willing to defy Trump, whose support he once highlighted in his campaign.
The prime minister has also made clear his unhappiness with Trump's decision to halt the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran launched in late February and instead pursue a settlement with the Tehran leaders.
In an interview that generated wide attention in the Arab world, Itamar Ben Gvir, the far-right national security minister in Netanyahu's cabinet, said that Israel should kill 30 to 40 people every night in Gaza.
"Not only those who endanger you right now. These are people who shouldn't be alive," he told a podcast.

Trump appeal in sex assault, defamation case rejected again
WASHINGTON – The US Supreme Court on Aug 17 rejected for a second time President Donald Trump’s attempt to overturn a jury judgment that he sexually assaulted and defamed writer E Jean Carroll.
The Supreme Court did not give any reason for its decision not to hear the president’s challenge. The court in late June also refused to hear Trump’s appeal against the original May 2023 verdict.
Carroll, 82, a former journalist and columnist, accused Trump of assaulting her in a dressing room of a New York department store in 1996.
Trump paid US$5.6 million (S$7.2 million) to Carroll in July after a civil jury found he sexually assaulted and defamed her.
When the allegations were published in a 2019 book she wrote, the Republican billionaire called Carroll a “nut job” and claimed she had fabricated her case.
In a separate defamation case in New York, Trump was ordered to pay US$83.3 million to Carroll. Trump has also appealed against that judgment to the Supreme Court. AFP

In the Rivne region, a 15-year-old girl wanted to take a photo on the railing of a road bridge, but lost her balance and fell from a height of about four meters, UNN reports, citing the police of the Rivne region.
Details
The incident occurred yesterday, August 16, at around 7 p.m. in the Berezne territorial community.
Juvenile prevention officers found out that the 15-year-old resident of the community was walking along one of the village streets with her 17-year-old sister. The younger girl decided to take a photo while sitting on the railing of a road bridge. However, she lost her balance and fell from a height of about four meters.

“We Are Preparing for War”: Poland Says Major Russian Provocation Could Be Months Away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
15:30:49 UTC
00:30:49 KST

- Category
- World
“We Are Preparing for War”: Poland Says Major Russian Provocation Could Be Months Away
Poland is preparing for the possibility of a full-scale war with Russia while warning that Moscow could stage a major provocation within the next several months, Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said, according to Polsat News on August 17.
Tomczyk said Poland’s government and military are no longer treating a confrontation with Russia as an unthinkable scenario.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Warsaw is actively planning for how the country would operate under the worst possible conditions, even as officials hope those preparations never have to be put into practice.
“We are preparing for war, hoping that it will never begin,” Tomczyk said.
Poland’s preparations extend well beyond its armed forces. According to the deputy minister, Warsaw is also strengthening the country’s energy sector and critical infrastructure against the possibility of future aggression.
Tomczyk pointed to the SAN counter-drone system being developed under Poland’s East Shield program, describing it as a major element of the country’s preparations and “a huge, state-of-the-art anti-drone system, the most advanced in Europe.”
He said most of the system is being designed specifically for wartime conditions rather than routine peacetime operations.
“Eighty percent of this system’s capabilities are being built for wartime; only a small part of it may be usable in peacetime conditions. We are not building an army for a press conference. We are building it with the understanding that it must be ready to conduct operations in defense of the state under extremely unfavorable conditions, and we must have the tools to do that,” Tomczyk said.
This warning comes amid reports that Russia established at least 10 new or upgraded drone facilities near its borders with Belarus and Ukraine, including launch sites that could eventually place NATO territory, including Poland and its capital Warsaw, within range of Moscow’s most advanced long-range attack drones.
At the same time, Polish officials believe a direct war is not necessarily the most immediate danger.
Tomczyk warned that Russia could carry out a large-scale provocation within months, although he did not specify what form such an operation might take.
He said Warsaw has changed the way it evaluates threats and no longer divides potential scenarios into those considered realistic and unrealistic.
“We no longer divide scenarios into realistic and unrealistic, only into probable and improbable. Today, I would no longer set a deadline. Even some large-scale provocation by the Kremlin could just as well happen within a few months,” Tomczyk said.
The warning comes amid growing concern in NATO about how quickly Russia could rebuild its military capabilities after its war of aggression against Ukraine.
Tomczyk referred to an assessment by NATO’s top commander in Europe, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, that Russia could restore enough military power by 2027 to pose a significantly greater threat to Europe.
Much, Tomczyk said, will depend on what happens in Ukraine.
“If this war ends, that would obviously be very good, but then it is highly likely that Russia will begin rebuilding its potential for the next armed conflict,” he said.
For Warsaw, supporting Ukraine is therefore directly connected to Poland’s own security.
Tomczyk argued that Russia is not currently prepared for a direct confrontation with NATO and would lose such a war, pointing to Ukraine’s ability to hold back Russian forces despite the enormous imbalance in resources.
“Today, Putin’s Russia is not ready for a confrontation with NATO and would lose such a war. All the more so because we can see that Ukraine has stopped Russia—let alone the full potential of the Alliance. We must be aware of our own strength. Use it, put our affairs in order, support Ukraine, and keep Russia as far away from us as possible,” Tomczyk said.

Pilots and Flight Attendants Face a Real Cancer Risk. Frequent Flyers Shouldn’t Panic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
15:30:03 UTC
00:30:03 KST

There is a particular unease that comes from seeing that an ordinary part of life has been linked to cancer. If you fly a few times a year, the results of a new study by two of us may elicit exactly that feeling; pilots and flight attendants die of radiation-related cancers at higher rates than workers in over 500 occupations that we studied.
So should you rethink your travel plans? We aren’t, and we don’t think you should, either. Understanding why can teach us a lot about how to read health headlines like this one.
Commercial jets cruise at altitudes above 30,000 feet, where the atmosphere is thin, allowing for higher speeds and engine efficiency. But the thinner atmosphere offers less shielding from cosmic radiation (in the form of high-energy particles that stream in from the sun and from deep space) than we enjoy closer to sea level.
Spending hundreds of hours among the clouds each year, air crew absorb more radiation, on average, than workers in any other job in the U.S.—including those generating nuclear power and our colleagues who work with radiation for medical purposes. This type of ionizing radiation, in sufficient doses, can damage DNA and give rise to cancer. What has never been clear is whether the amount aircrew accumulate over a career is enough to increase cancer risk above other occupations.
In a new study published in JAMA Internal Medicine, we set out to find that mark. Using federal data on nearly every death in the U.S., newly linked to each person’s usual occupation, we examined more than 12.7 million deaths from 2020 to 2024 (a majority of deaths among adults) across 503 occupations—an approach that earlier studies, which had mortality data on air crew but no other occupations, could not take.
The approach rested on simple logic. If cosmic radiation were truly driving cancer among air crew, the signal should appear specifically in the cancers that radiation is known to cause (breast, prostate, melanoma, and certain leukemias), and the signal should not appear in cancers like colon cancer that aren’t caused by this type of radiation. We would also expect to see higher rates of radiation-associated cancers among other types of workers exposed to radiation, like nuclear technologists. Meanwhile, unless something about aviation other than flying was associated with these cancers, we wouldn’t expect to see higher rates in aviation workers who remain on the ground, like aircraft mechanics and assemblers.
The pattern was hard to miss. Among all 503 occupations, flight attendants and pilots had the highest and second-highest share of deaths from radiation-related cancers—6.9% and 6.7%, respectively, after accounting for differences in age, sex, and other factors—a proportion that exceeded that of nuclear technologists. For cancers unrelated to radiation, aircrew sat near the middle of the pack. And our comparison groups fell exactly where the radiation hypothesis predicted; nuclear technologists ranked near the top, while ground-based aviation workers did not.
That internal consistency—seeing the types of cancers we expected in the workers we predicted would be most at risk, with control groups behaving precisely as expected—makes it unlikely that the pattern arose by chance. But as striking as these patterns are, this study, by itself, is not iron-clad proof of cause and effect. Our data cannot measure how much radiation any individual actually received. Occupations are sometimes recorded incorrectly on death certificates. People at higher baseline risk for this type of cancer may be more likely to work as pilots or flight attendants. Air crew face other hazards, from disrupted circadian rhythms to in-cabin exposures, that we could not fully account for.
Importantly, the study does not say that your next flight, or even a lifetime of flying for annual vacations, meaningfully raises your risk of cancer. The signal we detected generally reflects an entire career spent in the skies. To put this in perspective, pilots and flight attendants accrue an estimated 3 to 6 millisieverts of cosmic radiation each year, decade after decade. A traveler who takes 10 cross-country round-trip flights a year absorbs only about 0.4 millisieverts—roughly a seventh to 1/15 of what an aircrew member accrues in a single year, and only over a few years of heavy travel rather than an entire working life.
If anyone should take note, then, it is not passengers but the agencies charged with protecting the people who work at altitude. The Federal Aviation Administration already recognizes aircrew as occupationally exposed to radiation. Yet unlike nuclear workers, or air crew in Europe, U.S. pilots and flight attendants are subject to no federal dose limits and no requirement that their exposure even be monitored.
While our findings are unable to determine how large the risk is for any individual crew member, they do suggest that the workers who absorb the most radiation of any occupation in the country deserve the same basic protections we extend to everyone else who works around it.
So the next time a flight attendant hands you a coffee at 30,000 feet, there’s no need to fret over the tiny radiation dose you are taking on by being up in the sky. But do consider the doses they take on, day after day, and whether we are doing enough to look after the people who spend their careers somewhere the rest of us are only passing through.
