Iran signals readiness for ‘US ground operations’ as MoU expires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
14:15:17 UTC
23:15:17 KST

Iran signals readiness for ‘US ground operations’ as strategy shifts gear
Iran’s more offensive posture comes after Trump commented that the US would soon make the Strait of Hormuz its territory.
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have signalled they could shift to a more offensive approach to the war with the United States as a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Washington expires.
Brigadier General Yadollah Javani, head of the political bureau of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), told state television on Sunday night that his forces were ready to take whatever action is needed to defend the country.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4A US territory? Trump unveils proposal to control Strait of Hormuz
- list 2 of 4Did the US really destroy Iran’s ballistic missile capability?
- list 3 of 4Iran says no decision yet on a return to talks with the US
- list 4 of 4US aircraft carrier expected to relieve USS Lincoln in Middle East
Tensions between Iran and the US over control of the Strait of Hormuz have continued to rise despite a ceasefire being agreed between them in June. While the MoU effectively collapsed after fighting restarted last month, the agreement officially expires on Monday.
“The enemy started the war and our efforts have been defensive, although they might take on an offensive aspect,” said Javani.
He did not elaborate on what exactly the offensive measures could entail, but said opponents should expect “strategic surprises”.
IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi last week identified US and regional allies’ infrastructure – such as energy networks, power plants and internet-connected systems – as potential targets, if the US hits Iran’s civilian infrastructure.
Hardline Iranian politicians and media outlets have discussed the idea of mounting a ground incursion against US interests in Bahrain and Kuwait if Washington invades Iran.
Analysts have raised questions over the feasibility of that and the risks involved, while there is no recent indication that the US is planning ground operations in Iran.
The Iranian emphasis on offensive deterrence against the US comes after Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, viewed as a hardliner, consolidated his power by appointing several IRGC old guard and confidants to key military and security positions last week.
Khamenei said Major General Ahmad Vahidi’s rise to commander-in-chief of the IRGC must represent a mix of “maximum deterrence” with readiness for “powerful offensive operations against the enemy”.
Vahidi said Khamenei’s leadership and the Iranian armed forces had managed to “bring to its knees the most heavily-armed army in world history” after the US and Israel launched strikes in Iran on February 28, starting fierce fighting between the two sides.
US President Donald Trump reiterated on Friday his claim that Iran was defeated in the war while facing a naval blockade acting as a “wall of steel”. He also said the Strait of Hormuz would “pretty soon” be declared US territory.
The White House later suggested that comment was a joke, but Iran’s army chief, Amir Hatami, reacted by setting a $30,000 reward for any man who kills or captures a US soldier, if they are involved in any ground operation on Iranian soil. Women would be given twice the reward if they managed such a feat, he added.
“Our hands are open in terms of reaching the aggressors and they will become more open through our initiatives,” Hatami said, referencing recent Iranian attacks on US forces in Jordan.
Mohsen Rezaee, who has the powerful position of secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, suggested that the Trump administration might have been considering ground operations on Iranian territory, but held off as a result of “half-baked plans”.
Rezaee said that the US Central Command had refrained from hitting Tehran or northern Iran during the two-week flareup in fighting in July, instead attacking about 50 cities in 15 provinces.
He believed that the purpose of the air raids was to prepare for a ground assault to take control of the Strait of Hormuz and potentially reach nuclear facilities in Isfahan, where highly-enriched uranium is suspected of being buried under the rubble of US strikes.
Bridges, roads, maritime control towers, radar and other coastal installations, and military facilities were struck to cut off logistical supplies to southern Iran, Rezaee noted.
“They had not calculated that to land troops for the Strait of Hormuz, it’s not doable with 40,000-50,000 soldiers, you must bring at least 100,000 people,” he said. “You must cross the Zagros Mountains and be able to pass the Fars province.”
Iranian media and commanders have reported in recent weeks that scenarios are in place to defend individual islands and coastal areas in southern Iran that the US military might consider seizing. They include the critical oil export terminals on Kharg Island.
Iranian territories around the Strait of Hormuz have been reinforced with rapid-response units.
Army spokesman Mohammad-Reza Akraminia said last week that the aim will be to prevent any foreign troops landing on Iranian territory.
“If the Americans enter one of our islands, we will certainly target them on our own islands, let alone on other countries’ soil,” he told state TV.
Authorities have also signalled they are ready for any unrest provoked by separatist groups near Iran’s western borders with Iraq and Turkiye, or in the east with Pakistan and Afghanistan.
The IRGC has reportedly bolstered defences and continued to launch missile and drone strikes against armed groups based in Iraqi Kurdistan.
Iran shrugs off expired MoU
Javani, the political chief of the IRGC, said in a separate interview on Monday that the Strait of Hormuz will only fully reopen when Washington implements commitments agreed under the MoU signed in June.
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that a two-month window to halt fighting was not specifically mentioned in the MoU text. The ministry also dismissed that the expiration had any particular significance to the war with the US, or Tehran’s ongoing talks with Oman regarding Hormuz.
“It has been proven many times that the Islamic Republic of Iran is not a party to devise its policies under pressure, ultimatums and deadlines. We decide based on our evaluations of what guarantees national interests and security,” Baghaei told reporters during a briefing on Monday.
He said the talks with Oman have so far been delayed in producing an arrangement on the partial reopening of Hormuz due to legal and technical complexities, the multiple actors involved and “ill-wishing parties” seeking to spoil the process.
Parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said during a speech on Sunday night that the MoU was a “document of pride and victory in the field of diplomacy”.
Ghalibaf insisted that the Islamic Republic had emerged “victorious”, both politically and militarily, from the war with the US and Israel.
“I don’t mean that we destroyed their armies, I mean that they attacked us while clearly and repeatedly citing nine objectives, but did not achieve any of these goals at any level. That was the biggest abject failure for the US and the Zionist regime,” he said.
Ghalibaf has not yet managed to convince the Iranian leadership to agree on a long-term diplomatic resolution with the US to end the war.

Washington and Seoul have been conducting joint military exercises together since the 1950s as a deterrence to what Reed called North Korean aggression, and as a signal of strength to other potential adversaries.
Reed said Trump’s post contradicted a recent warning from NORTHCOM Deputy Commander Lieutenant-General Joseph Jarrard, that Pyongyang had successfully flight-tested intercontinental ballistic missiles with “enough boost to deliver a nuclear payload anywhere in North America”.
North Korea has not responded to Trump’s order, though it has previously voiced anger at the regular joint manoeuvres, which take place in South Korea.
The drills began as American allies in East Asia fret over North Korean displays of weapons capabilities and its growing alignment with Russia as well as traditional backer China. AFP

African Union rejects foreign interference in Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
14:07:27 UTC
23:07:27 KST

Breadcrumb
African Union rejects foreign interference in Sudan as it seeks new peace push
The African Union has rejected foreign interference and efforts to establish rival governments in Sudan, warning that outside involvement is prolonging a war that has fractured the country and displaced millions of people.
The message came as a delegation from the AU's Peace and Security Council began a two-day visit to Sudan, part of a renewed attempt by the continental body to press for a ceasefire, improve humanitarian access and revive a political process after more than three years of war.
Mohamed Khaled, the Algerian diplomat serving as the council's rotating chairman, delivered the position during talks with Sudan's army chief and Sovereignty Council chairman, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, at the presidential palace in Khartoum on Sunday.
Khaled condemned foreign interference in Sudan's affairs, saying such involvement "fuels the conflict", and rejected attempts to create parallel political entities that could threaten the country's unity and sovereignty.
"The only path to achieving lasting peace in Sudan is through dialogue, national reconciliation and reaching a comprehensive political settlement that meets the aspirations of the Sudanese people," he said, according to Sudan's Sovereignty Council.
The remarks come as Sudan has effectively splintered into competing zones of control. The Sudanese Armed Forces, led by Burhan, have regained control of much of Khartoum and central Sudan, while the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) remain entrenched across large parts of Darfur. Kordofan, which links central Sudan to the west and south, has emerged as another major battleground. Neither side, despite shifts on the battlefield, has achieved a decisive victory.
The RSF and its allies have also established the Sudan Founding Alliance, known as Tasis, a rival political structure opposed to the army-backed authorities. The AU has been trying to engage the political wings associated with both camps while resisting a formal partition of Sudan.
Khaled welcomed the army-backed government's return to operating from Khartoum, describing it as important for restoring state institutions and basic services. But he also called for a more inclusive transition, urging Sudan's government and political forces to work towards a national consensus that could eventually lead to a constitutional government chosen through free elections.
Prime Minister Kamil Idris told the AU delegation earlier on Sunday that a Sudanese-led national dialogue would "begin soon".
An AU return to Khartoum
The visit coincides with a broader effort by the African Union to restore a permanent political presence in Sudan after withdrawing its personnel when fighting engulfed Khartoum in April 2023.
The AU is moving to reopen its liaison office in the capital, a step that could give it a more direct role in mediation after more than three years of largely remote diplomacy. The office would also make the AU the only member of a five-member diplomatic grouping that includes the United Nations, European Union, Arab League and regional bloc IGAD to maintain a political presence inside Sudan.
The Institute for Security Studies said on Monday that the return presented the AU with a "narrow, but real" opportunity to exert greater pressure for a ceasefire and maintain direct channels with Sudanese political and military actors. But it warned that the organisation would have to avoid appearing aligned with Burhan's government simply because it is returning to the capital controlled by his forces.
That dilemma goes to the heart of the AU's latest intervention. Recognition from continental and international organisations would bolster the legitimacy of the army-backed government. But an effective mediation effort would require the AU to speak not only with Burhan's authorities, but with the RSF, civilian political movements, trade unions and other groups that have been largely sidelined by the country's armed factions.
The AU has repeatedly called for an immediate ceasefire, humanitarian access and an inclusive political process under African leadership. Its Peace and Security Council first laid out a roadmap for ending the conflict in May 2023.
But successive diplomatic efforts have failed to stop the fighting. The army and RSF agreed in Jeddah in May 2023 to commitments intended to protect civilians, followed by temporary ceasefire arrangements, but the deals repeatedly collapsed.
The war erupted in April 2023 after months of mounting tensions between the army and the RSF over control of the security apparatus and plans to integrate the paramilitary force into the regular military during a proposed transition to civilian rule.
It followed years of political turmoil after the overthrow of longtime president Omar al-Bashir in 2019 and the military's subsequent dismantling of a civilian-military power-sharing arrangement in October 2021.
Tens of thousands of people have been killed and millions uprooted since the conflict began, creating one of the world's gravest humanitarian crises.

DR Congo Ebola outbreak world's second-largest, deadliest in country's history
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
22:06:00 CST
23:06:00 KST

KINSHASA, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- The Ebola outbreak sweeping across the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has become the deadliest in the country's history and the second-largest ever recorded globally, with the World Health Organization (WHO) warning that it could eventually surpass the devastating 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic if it continues at its current pace.
The DRC has recorded 4,945 confirmed cases, including 2,325 deaths, since the current outbreak began, according to the latest figures released late Sunday by the country's health authorities. The case fatality rate stands at 47.0 percent, while 1,040 people have recovered.
According to WHO figures, the 2018-2020 outbreak in eastern DRC recorded 3,481 cases, including 3,323 confirmed cases, with 2,299 deaths and 1,162 survivors. It had previously been the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country's history.
The current epidemic has already grown significantly larger in terms of cases.
"It's already the second-biggest Ebola epidemic on record, and it's moving faster than any previous Ebola outbreak," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said at a press briefing in Geneva on Aug. 12, warning that "at its current pace, it's on track to eclipse the West African Ebola outbreak of 2014 to 2016."
The 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic, the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000, mainly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
OUTBREAK STILL ACCELERATING
Cases have now been detected in 55 health zones across six provinces -- Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uele, Tshopo, South Kivu and Bas-Uele. Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for 4,194 confirmed cases, or nearly 85 percent of the national total, and 1,838 deaths.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus, is the DRC's 17th recorded Ebola epidemic since the virus was first identified in the country in 1976.
The accelerating pace of transmission has increasingly alarmed humanitarian agencies.
"Ebola is winning in the DRC. We cannot let the virus outrun our response," UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said on Aug. 14 in a statement following an emergency meeting of the Inter-Agency Standing Committee, which brings together the world's major humanitarian organizations.
Fletcher described the outbreak as the fastest-growing on record and said it was killing someone roughly every 30 minutes.
He announced an additional 30.5 million U.S. dollars from the UN Central Emergency Response Fund, calling for a rapid expansion of treatment capacity, contact tracing and safe and dignified burials.
The UN official added that the response needs to double the number of safe burial teams and triple treatment capacity, while strengthening experienced management and basic services such as water, hygiene and healthcare.
RESPONSE STRUGGLES TO KEEP PACE
Despite efforts to scale up the response, major gaps remain in attempts to interrupt transmission.
The latest government situation report showed that contact follow-up had reached 85.3 percent nationally, but remained substantially lower in some affected areas. Authorities continued to cite weaknesses in alert reporting and in the listing and follow-up of contacts linked to confirmed cases.
Treatment facilities are also under pressure. Several Ebola treatment and transit centers in Ituri were reported saturated, while beds for suspected cases in North Kivu were fully occupied.
The operational environment adds another layer of difficulty. Many affected areas in eastern DRC have for years been hit by armed conflict, population displacement, weak infrastructure and limited access to healthcare.
Humanitarian agencies have also warned that the expanding Ebola response must not come at the expense of other major health emergencies.
Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), an international medical humanitarian organization, said Friday that measles, cholera, malaria and conflict-related health needs continue to affect large numbers of people in North Kivu and South Kivu.
More than 108,000 suspected measles cases and nearly 1,400 deaths had been reported nationwide by July 19, while more than 35,000 suspected cholera cases and over 1,000 deaths had also been recorded, according to figures cited by MSF.
"The Ebola disease outbreak is a major emergency, but it is not the only one," said Joshua Eckley, MSF head of programs in South Kivu.
For health authorities and international responders, however, the immediate race is increasingly against the trajectory of Ebola itself. ■

Feature: Chinese conservationist explores community-based wildlife protection in Kenya
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
22:05:20 CST
23:05:20 KST

Zhuo Qiang (L) talks with Simon Msago, a Maasai community leader in Ngoswani, in Narok, Kenya, Aug. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Liu Qiong)
NAIROBI, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- As dawn breaks over Ol Kinyei Conservancy in Kenya's Maasai Mara ecosystem, rangers are already combing the grasslands for signs of unauthorized entry and poaching while keeping a close watch on wildlife.
Among them is Chinese conservationist Zhuo Qiang, nicknamed "Simba," the Swahili word for lion. For him, this early-morning routine is driven by a broader mission to achieve human-wildlife coexistence.
In 2010, Zhuo left his job in China at the age of 37 and embarked on a less-traveled path: pursuing wildlife conservation in Kenya.
Without professional training in wildlife conservation, he found himself in a territory then dominated by Western organizations and local practitioners.
But Zhuo decided to stay. "I wanted to prove that Chinese people could also do wildlife conservation," he said.
Initially, Zhuo saw conservation largely through the lens of wildlife science: working in the field, studying animals and collecting data.
Living and working with Maasai communities changed that perspective. "The fate of wildlife was closely tied to the people sharing the same land," he said.
In the Maasai Mara ecosystem, livestock grazing is deeply connected to the livelihoods of pastoral communities. "If local people are asked to stop grazing but are given no alternative source of income, conservation cannot be sustainable," Zhuo said.
That principle laid the foundation for his work with the local community in establishing the Ol Kinyei Conservancy.
The area had suffered from prolonged overgrazing, with plants and the land itself deteriorating. Under the conservation model, local grazing land was leased and gradually restored, allowing vegetation to recover and creating a more suitable habitat for wildlife, said Zhuo.
Meanwhile, households participating in the scheme receive land-rental income and have access to jobs such as wildlife rangers and tourism workers. Their average annual income has increased from around 500 U.S. dollars to about 3,700 dollars, according to Zhuo.
Some residents from surrounding communities also learned from the experience and brought the approach back to their own grazing areas.
Nowadays, 26 private conservancies have been established around the Maasai Mara National Reserve, covering about 1,600 square km, according to Zhuo.
He believes the network of community conservancies provides additional safe space for wildlife to move and survive, extending conservation efforts beyond the boundaries of a single national reserve and into surrounding communities.
Simon Msago, a Maasai community leader in Ngoswani, said Zhuo's work encouraged more residents to take an active role in conservation.
In the past, many residents saw few direct benefits from wildlife conservation and had limited awareness of its importance. Today, community members are increasingly willing to work as rangers and protect wildlife, creating an effective layer of protection around the conservancies, Msago said.
"Human-wildlife conflict cannot be solved simply through restrictions and prohibitions. The key is to create alternative sources of income so that residents can gain tangible benefits from conservation," Zhuo said.
"That is what makes community-based conservation sustainable -- allowing local people to become part of wildlife conservation rather than bystanders with no stake in it."
While continuing his work in the Maasai Mara, Zhuo has also sought to strengthen exchanges between China and Africa in wildlife conservation.
In recent years, he has visited more than 30 nature reserves and national parks in China, sharing his experiences of community-based conservation in Africa with Chinese counterparts.
"Conservation practices in China and Africa each have their own characteristics, and there is much that the two sides can learn from each other," he added. ■

Saudi school textbooks drop vow to 'never give up Jerusalem'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Breadcrumb
'Muslims will never give up Jerusalem' dropped from Saudi school textbooks
Saudi Arabia has removed references to Palestine from some schoolbook maps and dropped language describing Israel as the "Zionist enemy", according to a new review of the kingdom’s textbooks, as efforts to revive the once fast-moving push towards Saudi-Israeli normalisation gather pace.
The revisions, covering textbooks used between 2024 and 2026, also include the removal of a sentence declaring that “Muslims will never give up Jerusalem”, according to the Israeli-based curriculum monitoring organisation IMPACT-se.
The changes are significant because they strip away language long used to affirm the importance of Palestine and Jerusalem to Muslims, as Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman continues a broader overhaul of the kingdom under his Vision 2030 programme.
They also arrive at a particularly sensitive moment. Saudi Arabia had been moving closer to a US-brokered normalisation agreement with Israel before 7 October 2023 and Israel's subsequent war on Gaza brought those negotiations to a halt.
Reports late last year suggested that diplomatic momentum around a possible agreement had begun to return, though Riyadh has publicly maintained that there would be no diplomatic relations with Israel without the establishment of a Palestinian state.
The latest textbook changes were first reported in Israeli media, including Maariv, which characterised them as evidence of a continued softening of Saudi attitudes towards Israel.
Among the most notable revisions is one in an 11th-grade Arabic-language textbook. An exercise in the 2023-24 edition included the sentence: “Muslims will never give up Jerusalem.”
The sentence disappeared entirely from editions published from the 2024-25 academic year onwards.
IMPACT-se interpreted its removal as eliminating a "politically and religiously charged reference to Jerusalem". But the revision is also notable for removing an explicit assertion of Muslim attachment to the city at a time when the status of Jerusalem remains one of the central disputes in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Another change appeared in an 11th-grade history textbook.
In its 2024-25 edition, Israel was referred to as the "Zionist enemy" in a section discussing King Salman's humanitarian activities and Saudi assistance to Egypt and Syria following the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.
By the 2025-26 edition, "Zionist enemy" had been replaced by "Israeli occupation".
The latter phrase still carries a clear political judgement and does not amount to recognition of Israel. But IMPACT-se described the change as a "reduction in the level of hostility" towards the country.
Perhaps more politically significant are changes to maps.
According to the review, the word "Palestine" had been removed from territory lying within Israel's internationally recognised borders in several textbooks. In some maps, the territory has instead been left unnamed.
The Israeli institute presented the revisions as part of a broader "moderation" of Saudi textbooks and a "reduction in hostility" towards Israel.
The New Arab has contacted the Saudi Cultural Bureau in London for comments.
Before the Gaza war, Saudi Arabia appeared closer than ever to joining the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Morocco in establishing formal relations with Israel under the diplomatic process begun with the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020.
In September 2023, just weeks before the 7 October attacks, Mohammed bin Salman said negotiations were bringing Saudi Arabia and Israel “closer” to normalisation “every day”.
Those efforts were effectively frozen after Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza, which devastated the enclave and sharply intensified public anger towards Israel across the Arab world.
Saudi officials subsequently hardened their public conditions for normalisation. Riyadh has repeatedly said it would not establish diplomatic relations with Israel without the creation of an independent Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital.
But reports since late 2025 have pointed to renewed efforts to revive the diplomatic track, with Washington continuing to view a Saudi-Israeli agreement as a major regional objective.

The next silicon? AI data centre material faces price spike amid China supply crunch
Beyond GPUs and memory chips, the rapid AI buildout is sparking demand for indium phosphide, a substrate used to power next-generation optical transmission
The artificial intelligence boom is driving demand for optical modules that enable ultra-fast data transmission in data centres, with the latest beneficiary a chemical compound that is seeing an unprecedented surge in prices.
Indium phosphide (InP) is used to make lasers that convert electrical signals into light, allowing data to travel rapidly through fibre-optic cables.
As a major producer of the material, China has seen prices climb sharply. According to a recent report by financial services firm Nomura citing industry experts, two-inch InP substrates surged to as much as 880 yuan (US$130.54) per wafer in June from as little as 500 yuan at the end of 2025. Over the same period, three-inch wafers rose to about 3,200 yuan from about 1,800 yuan.
An InP index compiled by financial information provider Wind, which tracks stock prices across more than 20 firms listed in mainland China, gained 4.2 per cent on Monday, steeper than some high-profile technology segments including lithography and semiconductor materials.
The industry was also mulling further price hikes that could reach 10 per cent in the fourth quarter of the year, according to a Monday report by Taiwan newspaper Economic Daily News.
Other Asian suppliers have followed suit. JX Advanced Metals, one of Japan’s leading InP substrate producers, was introducing a first round of revisions that could raise prices to two to three times previous levels, according to a report by JPMorgan earlier this month.
The investment bank said customer inquiries continued to exceed the company’s planned production capacity expansion.

Men face an elevated risk of suicide immediately following a relationship breakdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
14:00:24 UTC
23:00:24 KST

Following the end of a romantic relationship, men face an elevated risk of suicidal thoughts, attempted suicide, and death by suicide, with the highest risk occurring immediately after the split. These findings come from a massive global review published in Psychological Bulletin, providing a detailed look at how age, culture, and social isolation influence mental health after a breakup.
Around the world, men die by suicide at much higher rates than women. While many variables contribute to this disparity, the end of an intimate partnership is a recognized risk factor. Romantic relationships often provide essential emotional support, security, and a sense of belonging. When these bonds dissolve, people can experience profound psychological distress.
For many men, social expectations regarding masculinity can complicate this distress. Some traditional gender norms encourage self-reliance and emotional restriction, which can limit a person’s willingness to seek professional help. As a result, men often rely solely on their romantic partners for emotional intimacy. A breakup can lead to sudden social isolation and feelings of failure.
Despite the known association between breakups and mental health crises, details about which men are most at risk have remained poorly understood. To better investigate this pattern, Michael J. Wilson, a researcher at the University of Melbourne and Orygen in Australia, led a team to examine the specific variables that influence suicidal behavior in men after a relationship ends.
Wilson and his colleagues conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis. A meta-analysis is a statistical technique that combines the results of multiple independent studies to identify broad trends. The team searched academic databases for peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2023. They looked specifically for research comparing suicidal behavior among men based on their relationship status.
In total, the researchers gathered 75 studies spanning 30 countries. The combined sample size was massive, representing more than 100 million men. From this pool, 29 studies contained enough compatible data to be included in statistical meta-analyses. The remaining studies were analyzed narratively to identify common themes and demographic patterns.
The team examined three specific outcomes. These included suicidal ideation, which refers to having thoughts about or making plans for suicide. They also tracked data on suicide attempts, as well as recorded deaths by suicide.
The researchers first looked at non-fatal outcomes. Based on a pooling of available data, they found that separated or divorced men had 1.64 times the odds of experiencing suicidal ideation compared to married men. When looking at suicide attempts, the meta-analysis showed that divorced men had 1.73 times the odds of making an attempt compared to those who remained married.
The data on fatal outcomes revealed higher odds. Across the analyzed studies, divorced men had 2.82 times the odds of dying by suicide compared to married men. The risk was highly pronounced for younger men. Separated men aged 34 and younger faced more than eight times the odds of suicide compared to married men in the same age group.
The researchers also found that the timing of the relationship breakdown factored into the risk levels. Men in the state of separation, which typically represents the immediate aftermath of a breakup, showed nearly twice the odds of suicide compared to men whose divorces had been finalized. The data suggests that the acute emotional crisis of a fresh split poses the highest risk, which then tends to dissipate as time passes.
Cultural and socioeconomic variables played a role in the statistics as well. Divorced men in Asian countries displayed higher odds of suicide than divorced men in Western countries. The researchers note this could relate to cultural differences in family structures, child custody norms, and the social stigma associated with divorce in different regions. Additionally, men with less than a college education and those facing unemployment showed higher vulnerability.
The narratively synthesized studies pointed to underlying psychological themes connected to these breakups. Men who experienced intense shame, loneliness, and a loss of social networks after a split were heavily represented in the data. For some individuals, the breakup appeared to act as a sudden stressor that interacted with existing mental health conditions or substance use issues, leading to severe emotional dysregulation.
The source literature contained wide methodological variability, which prevented the researchers from including all 75 studies in the statistical meta-analyses. Many of the included studies also featured inconsistent reporting of demographic details. This limited the ability to run more specific statistical comparisons among different subgroups of men.
The bulk of the available research focused strictly on legal marital separation and divorce. There is comparatively little data tracking the mental health impacts of non-marital relationship breakups, such as the end of long-term cohabiting partnerships or dating relationships. The lack of data on non-marital splits means these findings primarily reflect the dissolution of formal marriages rather than all intimate relationships.
Future research will need to address these gaps by measuring relationship breakups more consistently across different types of partnerships. Investigators also recommend exploring the specific psychological mechanisms that cause a person to transition from suicidal thoughts to suicidal actions in the wake of a breakup.
The study, “Suicidality in Men Following Relationship Breakdown: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Global Data,” was authored by Michael J. Wilson, Amelia J. Scott, Vita Pilkington, Jacqui A. Macdonald, Simon M. Rice, John L. Oliffe, and Zac E. Seidler.

Record-early champagne harvest highlights climate change impact on French vineyards
- The Champagne region experienced its earliest grape harvest ever due to record heat and drought.
- Climate change has moved French grape harvests up by about 21 days over 50 years, causing lower yields with losses from frost, heat and drought.
- Champagne producers are adapting by using reserve stocks and may need to change practices, possibly altering champagne’s traditional taste and alcohol content.
AI generated
MONTGUEUX, France – In the Champagne region of north-east France, dozens of workers gathered among chardonnay vines at dawn on Aug 14, secateurs and buckets in hand, beginning the second day of the earliest harvest since records began in the early 20th century.
Climate changes such as the record heat and drought endured across swathes of Europe this summer are testing the resilience of France’s champagne industry. Higher temperatures accelerate ripening and produce grapes with a higher sugar content, making it harder to preserve champagne’s flavour and acidity.
This summer, the Champagne Committee (CIVC), the industry’s governing body, which determines harvest dates by monitoring grape maturity, advanced the official start date to Aug 12, more than a week earlier than 2025’s Aug 20.
“There’s no August vacation for winemakers,” laughed Benoit Velut, 39, owner of Champagne Jean Velut in the village of Montgueux, which produces about 28,000 bottles annually.
Behind him on the sloping vineyard in the south of the Champagne region, a couple of dozen seasonal workers moved swiftly along the vine rows. Their faces and arms were covered in dust and glistening with sweat in the early morning sun as temperatures climbed.
Velut’s father, Denis, 67, who handed over the vineyard to his son, said when he was a child, the grape harvest took place after school resumed.
“It used to be in late September and mostly in October, a time of year that was still pretty cool,” the older winemaker recalled.
“Back in the late 1990s, if someone had told me I’d be harvesting grapes before Aug 15, I would have said, ‘Come on, let’s be reasonable’,” he said.
Wine producers in other European countries, including Spain, have also begun their grape harvests much earlier than usual due to the scorching temperatures. Some fear heavy losses due to the impact of heat and drought.
Drought and heatwaves have brought additional burdens to a champagne industry already contending with weaker sales because of shifting consumer habits.
Vincent Finot, another winemaker in Montgueux, obtained special permission from the authorities to begin harvesting on Aug 6, the earliest date on record in all of Champagne, after tests showed the acidity of his grapes dropping sharply.
“I didn’t dare wait any longer,” he said, surprised by the exceptional earliness of this year’s harvest.
Rising temperatures have pushed French grape harvests progressively earlier over recent decades, experts said.
“On average, across all French vineyards, including those in Champagne, the harvest dates have moved up by about 21 days over the past 50 years,” said agroclimatologist Serge Zaka.
“The entire cycle of vines is affected,” Zaka said.
According to the Champagne Committee, around 30 per cent of the year’s crop was lost to spring frost. Heat and drought have further reduced yields.
Stephane Vignon, a winemaker in the village of Verzenay, said some bunches of grapes weighed nearly 30 per cent less than their typical weight.
Adapting methods
In anticipation of lower yields, champagne producers have relied on reserve stocks.
“We have implemented a system that allows us (in poor harvests) to reintroduce wines that are stored in tanks to replace the portion of the harvest lost,” said CIVC co-president Maxime Toubart.
Champagne’s challenges offer a sparkling opportunity to British winemakers.
Southern England’s chalky soil and more moderate temperatures, even if trending higher, mirror conditions in Champagne several decades ago. French champagne houses Taittinger and Pommery have both made investments.
Even though grape vines are historically “one of the most resilient species in France”, Zaka said, they will need to adapt to increasingly frequent climate shocks.
Traditional practices will need to evolve to preserve champagne’s acidity and quality, within the bounds of the appellation’s rules, he said. These might include planting more resilient grape varieties and maintaining ground cover to retain moisture.
Denis Velut said champagne might evolve towards wines that are warmer and higher in alcohol content.
“They might lose a little of that very ethereal, airy and light character that defines champagne,” he said. REUTERS

UN helped Iran expand anti-drug crackdown despite execution concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
14:00:05 UTC
23:00:05 KST

The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime has continued to support the Islamic Republic in identifying drug traffickers, despite concerns that those convicted in reportedly unfair trials are subjected to torture and, in many cases, executed.
The UNODC last week announced that it had “helped” Iran procure advanced detection scanners to combat methamphetamine trafficking at the country’s borders.
At least part of the technology was funded by Japan, according to a 2018 UN announcement, while the international body provided training to Iran’s Anti-Narcotics Police (ANP) and Customs Administration on how to use the technology and handled the international procurement and handover of the equipment.
Iranian seizures of meth increased from 30,393 kilograms in 2022 to 40,453 kg in 2025 with the help of the technology, according to the United Nations.
UN anti-drug assistance draws human rights scrutiny
Though presented by the UN as a major achievement in the thwarting of international drug trafficking, the agency’s official policy advocates for the universal abolition of the death penalty, viewing it as incompatible with fundamental human rights.
Nearly 1,000 out of the 1,212 executions for drug-related offenses in 2025 were carried out by the Islamic regime, according to the 15th report of Harm Reduction International published in March. At the time of the report, over 1,000 people were awaiting execution for drug-related offenses, some of whom had never come into direct contact with the illegal substance.
According to both the report and UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in Iran, Mai Sato, the large majority of those killed came from a background of poverty. Many were alleged to have worked in only minor roles in the drug trade, and they were denied proper due process during their trial.
Critics warn UN support may strengthen Iran and its proxies
Additionally, while the UNODC said last week that thwarting smuggling attempts helped stem the flow of money to organized crime groups, Anne Herzberg, legal adviser at NGO Monitor, told The Jerusalem Post that many of Iran’s proxies also rely on funds generated through illicit drug trafficking.
According to the IDF, Hezbollah has been funded through cocaine sales in Europe and is heavily involved in trafficking cannabis and Captagon along the Lebanese-Syrian border.
“It beggars belief that Iran is not aware of, does not profit off of, nor [is] heavily enmeshed in Hezbollah drug trafficking,” Herzberg said.
“Moreover, it appears Iran uses drug-related charges as a pretext to jail and execute dissidents,” he added.
UN Watch calls for safeguards on assistance
Hillel Neuer, the executive director of UN Watch, added that the UN “should not be helping Iran’s brutal regime catch people whom it may then torture into confessing and execute after sham trials.”
He noted that the Islamic Republic of Iran’s “fundamentalist government routinely denies defendants due process, and has dramatically increased executions for drug offenses, including in cases raising grave questions of innocence and coerced confessions.”
Neuer argued that the UN’s actions raise serious ethical and legal concerns if UN-provided technology is helping Tehran identify suspects “who may ultimately be sent to the gallows.”
Methamphetamine is the second most commonly found drug in people who fatally overdose in the US, according to research from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Acknowledging the need to fight drug trafficking was essential, Neuer said, nevertheless, that the UN cannot give “sophisticated tools to a regime notorious for torture, arbitrary detention and executions.”
“The UN needs to explain what safeguards it imposed, whether it tracks what happens to people arrested using its equipment, and whether it can guarantee that its assistance is not facilitating death sentences. If it cannot provide those guarantees, the assistance should stop,” he concluded.
The UNODC did not respond to The Jerusalem Post’s request for comment.

The COVID-19 vaccine may offer brain cancer patients a surprise benefit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

The COVID-19 vaccine may offer brain cancer patients a surprise benefit
A recent study adds to existing evidence that mRNA vaccines can prolong survival
The COVID-19 vaccine may give brain cancer patients a bonus shot at survival.
Patients who received the vaccine within 100 days before biopsy or tumor surgery lived twice as long as those who didn’t get the shot, scientists report July 31 at medRxiv.org. This link existed only for COVID-19 vaccines, not other vaccines that the team investigated.
The discovery suggests that the COVID-19 vaccine might be somehow firing up the immune system’s cancer-fighting powers, says James Markert, a neurosurgeon at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. But he’s quick to point out that his team’s paper, a preliminary study that has not yet been peer-reviewed, found an association between vaccination and survival — it did not show cause and effect.
Still, evidence is mounting that mRNA COVID-19 vaccines may spur anti-cancer action, says Elias Sayour, a pediatric oncologist at the University of Florida College of Medicine in Gainesville, who was not involved with the new study.
Last year, Sayour’s team linked mRNA COVID-19 vaccination with extended survival in patients with other types of cancer. People with lung cancer or melanoma who were vaccinated within a few months of immunotherapy lived nearly twice as long as their unvaccinated counterparts. The latest study adds more evidence to the pile. “I think it’s very interesting and I think it’s very important,” Sayour says.
Markert’s team examined data from 187 people with glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer with no cure. All patients had their brain tumors biopsied or surgically removed from 2022 to 2025. While half of those vaccinated before surgery lived 743 days or longer, for unvaccinated patients, the median survival was just 349 days. For glioblastoma patients, who have few treatment options, that amounts to an extra year of life.
The researchers tried to control for factors such as the severity of any COVID infections and whether COVID-vaccinated people had better health care than their unvaccinated peers. But it’s impossible to account for everything, Markert says, leaving it unclear exactly what is going on.
COVID vaccines may be rousing the immune system to come after cancer. Previous studies have hinted that mRNA-based vaccines in particular could be prompting this immune action. And in both Markert’s and Sayour’s studies, non-mRNA vaccines, like those for flu and pneumonia, did not give cancer patients the same survival boost.
In the case of the glioblastoma study, perhaps surgery itself is helping spark an immune effect, the researchers say. Before surgery, the cancer is hidden away in the brain. But it’s possible that cutting into the tumor releases bits of cancer proteins into the bloodstream, exposing it to the newly revved-up immune system.
The team wants to figure out if the vaccine acts like an alarm bell that wakes our immune defenders generally or a teacher instructing immune cells to specifically target glioblastoma. Preliminary data point to a possible role for teaching. mRNA COVID vaccines teach the immune system to recognize a snippet of coronavirus protein, and Markert’s team discovered a molecule on glioblastoma cells with a similar shape. So an immune lesson in spotting coronavirus might double as a lesson in spotting brain cancer.
Markert and his colleagues are now attempting to validate their findings in a different group of patients. If that pans out, he is interested in a clinical trial that directly tests how the COVID-19 vaccine affects brain cancer patients.
Sayour and his colleagues are already moving forward with a trial that looks at whether an mRNA COVID vaccine boosts the benefits of immunotherapy in patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer. If a large, randomized clinical trial were to one day show that a widely available and affordable vaccine like the COVID one extends cancer patients’ survival, that would be “earth shattering,” he says.
At this point, scientists cannot say whether that’s true or not. And no one is suggesting that cancer patients should delay surgery or other treatment until they get vaccinated, says Sivakrishna Uppalapati, a cancer researcher who works with Markert.
But when it comes to glioblastoma, Markert says he’s grateful for any new lead: “We think this provides hope.”

Japan’s slowing growth fuels policy divide between Tokyo, Bank of Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
13:57:27 UTC
22:57:27 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu, Emirhan Yilmaz and Emir Yildirim
17 August 2026•Update: 17 August 2026
Japan’s second-quarter growth of 0.3% on a quarterly basis and 1.1% on an annual basis fell short of expectations, fueling a policy divide between the Bank of Japan and Tokyo over how to handle the country’s rising inflation.
Exports were the main driver of growth, though a weaker yen limited their contribution. Weak domestic demand and capital spending also weighed on the economy.
The effects of the war in the Middle East also began to appear in Japan’s economic data.
The weaker-than-expected growth fueled expectations that the Bank of Japan’s room to tighten monetary policy could narrow.
Japan’s inflation rose from 1.4% in April to 1.5% in May and 1.7% in June, while it is expected to reach 1.9% in July.
The combination of weaker growth and rising inflation complicates Japan’s economic policy path. The Bank of Japan plans to raise interest rates because of inflationary pressures, while Tokyo favors further fiscal expansion in response to slowing growth.
Asian markets analyst Sadi Kaymaz told Anadolu that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s falling approval ratings and the cost of living should also be considered when predicting what may come next.
“These factors keep fiscal expansion and additional spending on the agenda, but the bond markets aren’t receptive to additional spending, and they see it as contrary to fiscal health, demanding a higher risk premium,” Kaymaz said.
The Bank of Japan was “more concerned over inflation and felt more confident about wage increases and growth, but we can say that with the release of this growth data on Monday that this confidence may have somewhat waned,” he said.
Kaymaz added that the data would have to show continued cooling in growth to cause concern.
He said Japanese inflation is generally supply-driven, meaning weakness in demand should be considered secondary, while inflationary pressures continue in imports of raw materials and intermediate goods.
Kaymaz said wage increases are continuing and real wages are a key condition for ensuring sustainable and healthy inflation, adding that it is too early to discuss the risk of recession or disinflation.
“We should also pay attention to artificial intelligence developments,” he said. “Japan’s semiconductor sector is strong and the investment environment stays vibrant — if there was a sudden pullback or freeze in AI investments, the recession possibility could increase.”
“I’d like to say once again that the quarterly data does not point to a recession risk yet,” he added.

Travertine Extends Banyoles’ Historic Urban Landscape in Spain
In Banyoles, Spain, MIAS Architects completes the latest phase of its long-term refurbishment of the historic town center, extending the intervention to Plaça d’en Ges and the surrounding streets of Sant Martirià and Sant Antoni. The project continues an urban strategy developed over several decades, using locally sourced lacustrine travertine as the primary material for streets, public spaces, furniture, and landscape elements.
The project began with an initial sketch approximately 30 years ago, followed by the first construction phase two decades ago. The latest intervention continues the approach established in the original scheme, in which travertine was used to repave medieval streets and squares while exposing the historic water canals and creating a continuous pedestrian landscape. In the new phase, the material is extended beyond the horizontal plane to form benches, edges, planting beds, and changes in level.
all images by Pau López
Carved Stone Reorganizes Plaça d’en Ges and Surrounding Streets
Large travertine blocks are cut, fractured, and carved to reveal different layers within the stone. Their surfaces alternate between smooth horizontal planes and rough vertical cuts, creating a material language that references the surrounding facades, water channels, and geological strata. Around the existing plane tree and cast-iron fountain in Plaça d’en Ges, the travertine forms a continuous perimeter that defines a smaller urban space within the square. The former traffic island is reorganized as a pedestrian area, with the stone simultaneously functioning as paving, seating, landscape edging, and planting infrastructure.
The intervention by MIAS Architects design studio extends the same material palette across the square and adjacent streets, allowing the individual elements to remain part of a coherent urban system. Emerging stone-cutting technologies are combined with traditional craftsmanship and on-site adaptation, enabling individual blocks to be configured according to their specific position and function.
The project treats paving, furniture, and planting as interconnected components of the public realm. Travertine blocks establish thresholds, seating areas, level changes, and small planted spaces, allowing the material to operate at different scales throughout the intervention. The streets and square are reorganized as a continuous surface that clarifies pedestrian movement and softens changes in level. Previously fragmented or residual areas are incorporated into the pedestrian network, transforming narrow streets into civic routes and defining Plaça d’en Ges as a more contained urban space. The material strategy also maintains a close relationship with the scale of the surrounding historic buildings. Minimal metal detailing and discreet lighting complement the travertine without introducing additional visual elements that compete with the existing urban fabric.
MIAS Architects completes the latest phase of Banyoles’ historic center refurbishment
Long-Term Material Strategy by MIAS Continues Across Banyoles
The latest phase extends the architectural language established by the earlier refurbishment, using the same local stone in new forms and applications. Its transformation from paving into seating, retaining edges, planting beds, and other urban elements demonstrates how a consistent material system can adapt to changing spatial requirements while maintaining continuity across different phases of construction. By combining digital stone fabrication with traditional techniques and site-specific adjustments, MIAS Architects continues to develop the potential of lacustrine travertine as both a construction material and an organizing element for public space. The completed intervention reinforces the long-term strategy of establishing a coherent pedestrian landscape across Banyoles’ historic center while connecting the town’s material history with contemporary methods of urban design.

UK government ‘irresponsible’ for not publishing emergency drought plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
13:56:49 UTC
22:56:49 KST

The UK government has been accused of a lack of transparency and of acting irresponsibly for refusing to publish the emergency drought plans that are produced by water companies.
Water firms are required to publish statutory drought plans every five years to detail the actions needed to ensure public water supply is maintained and the environment is protected during drought.
Water levels at five key reservoirs in England and Wales are now “exceptionally low” and three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales are in drought.
The 2027-32 drought plans, which are under consultation, detail what will happen in different scenarios, with the most extreme actions ranging from standpipes in the street to rota cuts, where water is limited to a few hours each day.
Alongside these publicly available plans, water companies are required to produce separate emergency drought plans.
A water industry source said these plans were not published to avoid alarming the public. The government said the plans were not published for security reasons.
Alastair Chisholm, the water, policy, regulation and governance lead at the consultancy firm Arup, said that in the “new normal” of the climate crisis causing droughts to become more frequent and more extreme, there would probably be situations where “some quite difficult decisions need to be taken with some quite significant imposition’s on people’s lifestyles”.
He pointed to Day Zero in Cape Town, South Africa, in 2018, when millions of households faced drastic water shortages after the worst drought to hit the city in almost a century.
“People do genuinely start to be scared that they’re not going to be able to get water to drink, and that has got all manner of sort of social connotations which is going to need to be very carefully managed,” Chisholm said.
Prof Liz Bentley, the chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, said it made sense not to publish these plans because drought could lead to widespread impacts on certain critical industries. For example, recent drought and extreme heat in Europe forced several nuclear power plants to shut down.
“If you start to see significant shortages of water that impact major industries then these are the kind of things you want to keep confidential because that could have widespread effects on the security of the country,” Bentley said.
In some areas of England, the impact of water shortages is already being felt. Sussex, Cambridgeshire, Suffolk and Norfolk have all seen housing and business development delayed due to water supply availability and ageing or inadequate water infrastructure.
Water shortages are also affecting food security, with global food prices at a three-year high as heatwaves, drought and war push up the cost of crops.
With water increasingly becoming a scarce commodity and as demand for water increases due to the rapid growth of water-hungry industries such as datacentres, the trade body Water UK recently told the Guardian it had asked the government to publish a drought hierarchy to set out which sectors would be prioritised in times of water shortages, but that ministers had yet to do so.
“Without this there will be a trade-off across society,” said Jon Chappell, Water UK’s deputy director.
Ollie Hayes, the head of big tech and campaigns at the campaign group Global Action Plan, said that amid increasing concern that datacentres could be prioritised over other sectors for water, it was irresponsible for the government to keep its emergency drought plans from the public.
“People are deeply anxious about dwindling water supplies and want to know what the plan is. Will water-hungry AI datacentres be prioritised in a drought emergency? The secrecy only adds to a sense that controversial decisions like this may have already been made,” he said.
The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said it was “deeply worrying that emergency drought plans are being hidden from the public”. “People deserve to know what plans – if any – are in place to protect our water supply,” he said.
Polanski said full nationalisation of water companies must be at the top of the government’s agenda to “prevent catastrophic water shortages in the years ahead”.
On Sunday it was reported that the industry regulator, Ofwat, was considering allowing water companies to raise bills during periods of drought.
Amy Fairman, the head of campaigns at campaign group River Action, criticised the government’s overall lack of transparency over how the country will deal with drought as the climate crisis intensifies.
“My key concern is around the lack of a holistic plan to deal with water shortages going forward. There is no more precious resource than water, and yet there isn’t a national water security plan in place,” she said.
The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said emergency drought plans were in addition to publicly available statutory drought plans and would not be published for security reasons.
A Water UK spokesperson said: “Each water company publishes a drought plan, which is consulted on publicly and sets out the actions the company will take at each stage of a drought. Planning for a severe drought sits under a separate framework, and publication is a matter for government. We support calls from the House of Lords environment and climate change committee for the government to decide how water should be prioritised in a severe drought.”

Yemen’s Ansar Allah group, also known as the Houthis, claimed Monday that its forces had targeted several Saudi naval vessels, along with a weapons depot, in a wide-ranging missile and drone barrage.
In a statement posted on Telegram, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said a Saudi amphibious transport ship and several accompanying naval vessels had been successfully struck in an aerial attack involving “a number of” ballistic missiles
Describing the missile strike as “precise,” Saree said that several of the targeted ships had been sunk, while the rest had caught fire as a result of the attack.
Houthi forces also targeted a Saudi weapons depot in the Sahn al-Jin camp, located in Yemen’s central-eastern Marib province, with multiple drones, the spokesman added.
The claims had not yet been confirmed by the Saudi authorities. 
Later, the independent news website Al-Masdar Online reported that “the Houthi militia targeted a civilian vessel owned by a Yemeni contractor with four consecutive missiles at Al-Ardi Port in the Bab al-Mandab area on Monday morning.”
Citing unnamed sources, the website said the vessel, named Amir Khan, is owned by Yemeni contractor Bilal al-Shumairi, who previously purchased it from an Indian trader in Indonesia for use in his maritime and commercial activities.
The sources said the vessel was “completely empty of commercial cargo when it was targeted,” as it had been docked at a maintenance berth since December 2025 and was undergoing periodic maintenance and rehabilitation.
“All the vessel’s crew members are Yemeni nationals and had completely evacuated it during the past week, preventing any casualties among them,” the sources added.
The missile attack caused “extensive damage to the vessel and widespread destruction at the berth where it was docked, rendering it nearly inoperable,” the sources said.
In 2014, the Iran-backed Houthis overran much of the country, including Yemen’s capital, Sanaa.
This was followed by several years of war between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces backed by a Saudi-led coalition. 
Since the eruption of the Israel-Gaza conflict in 2023, the Houthis have become increasingly involved in regional hostilities, carrying out missile attacks on Israel and Israel-linked commercial shipping in the Red Sea.
The latest uptick in fighting – coupled with the ongoing conflict between Iran and the US – has revived fears of a return to full-scale conflict in impoverished Yemen.

Ukrainian volunteer flies to Russia to save his 18-year-old son after being blackmailed by FSB
Ukrainian volunteer Mykhailo Puryshev has said that Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) used his 18-year-old son to blackmail him, prompting Puryshev to travel to Russia in an attempt to save him.
Source: a statement by Puryshev on Instagram and a comment from his team
Quote from Puryshev: "They [the FSB] suggested that we 'make friends'. There were two options: either I cooperate with them and they help my son and leave him alone, but I would betray my country and my children here; or I refuse to cooperate and they kill my son. I decided I had a third option – to go there, and once I'm with them, they can do whatever they want, but my son will stay alive, and I hope they will leave him alone."
Details: Puryshev has two children from his first marriage who live in Russia with his ex-wife.
He said he received the first call from his son's phone number on 16 July 2026. The caller introduced himself as "the equivalent of your security service".
There were four more calls, this time from a different number, during which the caller asked Puryshev to disclose the positions of Ukrainian units and provide information to Russia. Puryshev recorded all the conversations.
An excerpt from the recording of the first call:
The caller began the first conversation: "I've come to visit your son."
Puryshev: "If I don't cooperate with you, you're going to send my son to the trenches?"
Caller: "You understand correctly… If you attempt to tell anyone about us, the consequences will be the same."
During the conversations, Puryshev was offered help with resolving all of his son's problems and financial assistance for him. The caller also repeatedly promised to let him speak to his son, but none of these promises were kept.
During the five calls, Puryshev did not provide any information and refused the offers of money.
He then decided to travel to Russia in an attempt to save his son.
In a statement, the volunteer's friends said: "The FSB set one condition – silence. So publicity is the only defence for Mykhailo and his son."
Background:
- Mykhailo Puryshev is a businessman from Mariupol. In March 2022, as a volunteer, he made six trips to besieged Mariupol to evacuate people to Zaporizhzhia. He and his team subsequently helped evacuate over 1,000 people. He was detained by Russian occupying forces but later released.
- After Mariupol, Puryshev and his team built invincibility centres along the entire line of contact, from Kupiansk to Kherson Oblast, including in Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Kurakhove. [Invincibility centres are heated premises stocked with food and power banks to assist residents facing hardships due to power cuts – ed.]
- A year ago, Puryshev and some of his fellow volunteers voluntarily joined the Ukrainian defence forces. He served as a UAV crew commander and is now being discharged from service on health grounds after suffering two heart attacks.

A new generation of Catalans tries to rekindle the independence movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
13:53:35 UTC
22:53:35 KST

A new generation of Catalans tries to rekindle the independence movement
Nearly 10 years after the attempted referendum on Catalan independence which led to violent clashes between the public and the police, the political demands of the independence movement have not been met. ENTR travelled to Catalonia in June to meet with young people there who are continuing the fight to preserve Catalan identity – not with politics, but with culture.
Issued on: Modified:
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
“The only Spanish thing about me is my identity card.” That is one of the first things Pau told us. We met the former Catalan independence activist in Celra, a village near Girona in Catalonia, where he grew up. Catalan independence has been a point of contention for centuries. As soon as you set foot in this region of northern Spain, it’s easy to understand why its inhabitants see Catalonia as a nation in its own right, with a distinct language, flag, culture, architecture and customs.
After numerous political attempts to establish Catalonia as an independent territory, young Catalans have now turned to culture to fight for their identity.
Celebrating Catalan identity at Cabro Rock
To see this for ourselves, we travelled to Vic, the town that hosts the Cabro Rock festival every year. The aim of this festival is to promote Catalan music and identity. Once we arrived we quickly realised that here, Catalan is king. It was almost impossible to get a reply in Castilian, Spain’s official national language, and hundreds of red and yellow-striped flags flew among the food trucks and drinks stalls.
“Visca Barça and Visca Catalunya lliure!”, chanted Joan as he welcomed us to the festival. Joan, alias KZU Music, was performing as a DJ on the night we went to Cabro Rock. He has been pro-independence since childhood, and his way to express it has always been music and language. A couple of years ago he made a name for himself on social media by remixing traditional Catalan music. For the 27-year-old artist, preserving his language is a political act: “Under my posts [on social media], there are lots of comments saying: ‘You’re doing more for the Catalan language and for Catalonia than most Catalan politicians’,” said the DJ with a smile.
Festival-goers seek out this event precisely to show their engagement with the Catalonian cause: “Now that there are so many Catalan bands, we need to support them. [...] I think it’s good that not everything happens in Barcelona. We’re from central Catalonia, and it’s cool to see that that’s appreciated too. It’s very important!”
A political standstill
The atmosphere at Cabro Rock was festive, but Catalans have endured years of political struggles, which have often ended up in violent confrontations.
On October 1, 2017, despite the Spanish government’s crackdown on the vote, more than two million Catalan people participated in the referendum that would decide on the region’s independence status.
At the time, Pau was part of an extremely active pro-independence student union that helped organise the referendum. “I think that in 2017, the general feeling was that we couldn’t get anything from Spain, that it would make no concessions…This project of independence allowed us, in the first place, to freely decide on the future of Catalonia, to know if it would become an independent state. But it also had the goal of bringing more democratic change, bettering education, healthcare... A number of issues that we thought we could work on with independence.”
But the Spanish government did not take it well. The referendum was declared unconstitutional, Catalonia’s autonomy was suspended and direct rule was imposed in the region. This resulted in unprecedented protests as people rose up in dissent.
“Looking back, what I feel is pride in the people from my town and in Catalans in general for what we have achieved. I think it was one of the most important and massive demonstrations that Europe has seen in the past several years. For me, it’s an act of civil disobedience which, considering the number of people who came together and the way it happened, was pretty much unprecedented in Europe,” recalled Pau.
Two years after this unprecedented event, on October 14, 2019, 12 of the Catalan leaders who had organised the referendum were tried, with some facing charges of sedition and embezzlement of public funds. Nine were convicted.
It was at this point that many pro-independence activists began to turn their backs on politics, weary of their leaders’ broken promises and the lack of renewal within the pro-independence political class.
Reviving their language
Today, Pau believes that the only thing left for young people in his region to fight for is their language: “Due to the boom in tourism in Barcelona, it has become increasingly difficult to do things in Catalan. In other words, when I go there, I sometimes find myself in situations where people don’t understand me when I order a coffee in Catalan. But I think it’s also up to the authorities to ensure that everyone can address us in our language, so that we can be welcomed at hospitals, in pharmacies and in bars, in Catalan,” said the activist.
But Pau noted that more and more young people are committed to saving Catalan: “Nowadays, many young people, even those who don’t talk about independence, talk a lot about the language. They make music in Catalan, produce films in Catalan, or create TikTok content exclusively in Catalan. That gives us hope.”
This mission to preserve Catalan language and culture could breathe new life into the independence movement. That, at any rate, is what Joan hopes: “My hope for Catalonia is that people start realising that Catalan is our language, that they understand that if we don't speak it, nobody will. That it’s super important to speak everyday, to make everybody who comes here understand that our language is Catalan. And of course, at some point, I would love to think that we will get independence.”
Today, Catalan is spoken by more than 10 million people in Europe, including more than eight million in Spain, mainly in Catalonia. However, this language is still neither recognised as a national language of Spain nor of the EU; it is merely an official regional language. The Catalan people’s fight for recognition continues on the cultural battlefield.

AL wild-card race looks like a mess. It could be lots of fun
The middle of the American League standings has turned into a medicore mess.
It might make for a fascinating playoff race.
There are seven teams fighting for the final AL wild-card spot and all of them have a record below .500. The Baltimore Orioles would make the playoffs if the season ended Sunday, sporting a 61-63 record.
Right behind them: The Texas Rangers (61-64), Toronto Blue Jays (61-65), Detroit Tigers (60-64), Minnesota Twins (60-65), Cleveland Guardians (60-65) and Seattle Mariners (59-66). The Houston Astros could be in the mix as well with a 63-62 record that gives them a narrow advantage in the AL West.
Many of those teams were sellers at the trade deadline this month. The Blue Jays traded outfielder Daulton Varsho to the Astros, the Orioles traded former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman to the Red Sox and the Tigers dealt ace Tarik Skubal to the Dodgers and right-hander Casey Mize to the Padres.
Now at least one of those teams might find itself playing baseball in October anyway.
Only three teams in MLB history have made the playoffs with a losing record and all of them happened during seasons when the schedule was much shorter than normal.
The 1981 Kansas City Royals (50-53) qualified for the postseason thanks to a split-season format caused by a players’ strike during the middle of the summer. In 2020, the Houston Astros and Milwaukee Brewers both squeezed into the playoff bracket with a 29-31 record during the pandemic-shortened season that had an expanded playoff field of 16 teams.
Trivia question
Joshua Báez became the first player to hit three home runs in his big-league debut, leading the Cardinals to an 8-4 victory over the Chicago Cubs on Saturday.
Only seven players have hit even two homers in their first regular-season game in the majors since 1900. Who are they?
The workhorse returns
Miami Marlins ace Sandy Alcantara has had a great bounce-back season with a 13-7 record and 3.43 ERA after struggling last year following Tommy John surgery that caused him to miss the 2024 season.
He’s also doing what he does best — pitch deep into games.
The 2022 National League Cy Young winner has already thrown 170 2/3 innings this year, which leads the big leagues by a large margin. If he continues at this pace, he’ll throw roughly 220 innings in 2026.
Throwing more than 200 innings has become increasingly rare over the past few decades as teams lean more on their bullpens. Only three pitchers reached the mark last season — Logan Webb, Garrett Crochet and Cristopher Sanchez.
Just 20 years ago in 2006, there were 45 pitchers who hit 200 innings.
If Alcantara manages to make it to 220 this season, that will be most in the big leagues since — Sandy Alcantara. He threw 228 2/3 innings during 2022 when he won the Cy Young.
Dodgers in the dumps
The Los Angeles Dodgers are the two-time defending World Series champs and one of the favorites to win the title again this season.
They sure aren’t playing like these days.
Los Angeles is 5-11 in its past 16 games, having been swept by the Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs and losing series to the Arizona Diamondbacks and Milwaukee Brewers in that span. Since July 1, the Dodgers are 18-21.
“I say this because it’s just been four or five, six weeks of below average production in our offense. It’s just the truth, and I think we have just haven’t played clean baseball for quite some time, and that speaks to the defense,” manager Dave Roberts said.
The Dodgers have a chance to gain some momentum this week with three games against the Colorado Rockies and three more against the Pittsburgh Pirates. The Rockies are in last place in the NL West while the Pirates have fallen to 61-65 after a promising start to the season.
Trivia Answer
Jose Fernandez (D-backs, 2026), Chase DeLauter (Guardians, 2026), Trevor Story (Rockies, 2016), J.P. Arencibia (Blue Jays, 2010), Mark Quinn (Royals, 1999), Bert Campaneris (Kansas City Athletics, 1964), Bob Nieman (Browns, 1951)

‘This is probably my last year in football,’ says Cristiano Ronaldo
RIYADH (AP) — Cristiano Ronaldo says this Saudi Pro League season is likely to be the last of his professional career.
The 41-year-old superstar’s contract with Riyadh club Al-Nassr, signed in December 2022, expires next June, and he has told Vogue magazine that another is unlikely.
“This is probably my last year of football, and I want to leave a spectacular legacy,” Ronaldo said.
The Portugal forward, who has scored 976 career goals, married long-time partner, Georgina Rodriguez, earlier this month.
“I have my future all mapped out,” he said. “I have so many things to keep me busy that to tell you just one thing is hard. Because football could leave a big hole, you have to fill your time in various ways, not just one.

The 2026-27 SPL season is Ronaldo’s 25th as a professional. During his career, he has won five Ballon d’Or awards and five UEFA Champions League titles.
Ronaldo’s 28 league goals last season helped Al-Nassr become champion of Saudi Arabia in May to secure his first trophy since arriving in Riyadh, and a first league title for the club since 2019.
After returning from his wedding, he missed Al-Nassr’s first game of its title defense on Saturday, watching from the sidelines as it opened with a 3-0 win over Al-Fateh.
“Cristiano is here today, and he is always present with us,” Al-Nassr coach Ange Postecoglou said after the game.
Ronaldo could play against Al-Diriyah in the King’s Cup on Tuesday.
“The most important thing now is recovery, especially as we have only two days after this match,” former Tottenham Hotspur and Nottingham Forest coach Postecoglou said.
Ronaldo’s comments came days after long-time rival Lionel Messi revealed that, following his father’s death, he may soon retire.
“I don’t know how to carry on,” Messi, 39, said. “I used to just play football, and now I’m really not sure if I’ll carry on doing it for much longer.”
